# `afkconvoy`

afkconvoy works a repo's ready GitHub issues unattended. One host runner, started by `afkconvoy run`, holds one fleet instance per repo. Each dispatches a worker per issue — a coding agent in its own git worktree — and lands finished PRs on the base branch through the gate and landing turns. Fleet state lives in GitHub and the repo's remote; no process holds it.

`afkconvoy --help` answers the index: this guide, then each command's one line under who runs it, then each topic's first sentence. `afkconvoy help all` answers the whole manual: guide, commands and topics in full. `afkconvoy -h` lists commands on one screen.

## What it needs

- A config on the base branch: the first yaml block of docs/agents/afkconvoy.md. A repo whose config names a team is a bound repo: its workflows say how issues are worked. One whose config names none is unbound: one worker per issue, then a turn that lands its PR.
- A private tracker for the issues the fleet reads and writes. Only a private repo can be its own tracker: anyone who can comment writes what workers read. Settle it with the user: [`afkconvoy help first-start`](help:first-start).
- Host settings apply to every fleet; `run` changes those named. Defaults: host sleep 00:00-06:00 local time after host and fleets idle 10 minutes (`--no-host-sleep` required off macOS); watch workers above half the cores (at least one) for two minutes, a quarter of memory resident, or a tenth of free disk written in ten minutes (at least one GiB); admission holds starts above 200% load per core or below 10% memory or 1% disk free, calling for the watch after 600 seconds held for one reason or memory pressure; end exclusive commands after 1200 seconds holding others up; panel port 7070 (a free port if taken); the host runner looks every 300 seconds in the operator's directory, or the stock watch's by default. Concurrency: 3 claims at work per checkout. Flags: `afkconvoy run --help`.
- `gh` logged in as a user who may push to the repo.
- `orca` on the PATH: every worker is started through it. It is running (`orca open`) and was given this checkout, once (`orca repo add --path "$PWD"`).
- `claude` on the PATH and logged in, when it is what starts a worker.
- `pi` there too, holding credentials for a provider (`/login` at its prompt), or `codex`, logged in (`codex login`): each when a stage or a patrol is on it, only then.

`plan`, `tick` and `run` check these first. With one missing, logged out, not running or not given the checkout they do nothing and the error gives the line to run for each: nothing is installed, started or added for you.

## What to run first, in a checkout of the repo

1. `afkconvoy checkouts`: if this checkout is absent, read [`afkconvoy help first-start`](help:first-start) and settle the first start with the user before `run`.
2. `afkconvoy config`: read the config, what the fleet goes by. Its `--help` shows one whole. Then `afkconvoy check`, only in a bound repo: does the team load? A team is designed first: see designing a team, below.
3. `afkconvoy plan`: what a tick would act on. It changes no fleet state, but may push and delete a startup probe on the remote. To read without writing anything, run `afkconvoy doctor`.
4. `afkconvoy run`: the checkout's fleet instance, held by the host runner until it is stopped. It answers once the first tick ended.

To watch a running fleet, checking on it every few minutes, run `afkconvoy doctor --all --since <until of your last look>`. A first look runs `afkconvoy doctor --all` without `--since`; its `until` is where the next look starts.

Every host watches itself: in the operator's directory where `afkconvoy run --watch-dir <dir>` names one, otherwise as the stock watch in afkconvoy's own directory. Its host runner takes that look every five minutes, with no model, and when it holds something an operator would act on, starts one watch — an agent session in that directory, given the look — continued on another harness where its own gives out. `afkconvoy run --help` says when, and `doctor` says the watch running and what the last one did.

A watch is the operator for every repo on the host's checkout list. It trusts worktrees, restarts, nudges, continues or switches workers and changes host settings; once a fleet fault is fixed it hands the escalated issue back with the line `doctor` names and checks the next tick dispatches it. It may change any listed repo in a checkout of its own, land it in that repo's turn with `land --watch`. Where the fix must reach an installed tool, it has that repo's fleet cut a version after landing, lets the host runner move onto it and checks the fault on the new version. Human decisions stay with the human, untouched and listed in the watch's record; what it prints records each fix, PR, cut, check and anything still pending. It acts only on what the fleets own, preserves what cannot be rebuilt and changes no base branch outside a landing turn. Its sessions together have one hour.

And whenever something looks wrong: `afkconvoy doctor` — it changes nothing, and names each fix.

After rules, Jev judges screens sent to TypeSafe only with `run --jev-key-command`. Without a key or settled answer, workers go to the operator and watch: `help roster`.

## What a command answers

Every command prints exactly one JSON object on stdout. A failure is {"error": …} with a non-zero exit — and "see" beside it, where a topic explains it: the command that prints that topic. Warnings go to stderr. A few print otherwise: `show` a drawing unless asked about an issue, `help` Markdown as `--help` does, `skill` the text of a file, `guard` answers as a hook does, with its exit code, and `exclusive` as its command does. A fleet instance prints nothing: it logs a line as each tick starts and one as it ends, in its tick log.

## The commands, by who runs them

Read `afkconvoy <command> --help` before first running it. Commands are grouped by who runs them:

- **Run by the operator** — `config`, `check`, `plan` before `run`; `tick` for one pass, `stop` to stop; `doctor --all --since <until of your last look>`, `checkouts`, `panel` to watch (`doctor` names each fix); `kit`, `cast`, `switch` for workers' harnesses and models; `patrol-now` to run a patrol now; `takeover` to take another fleet instance's claims.
- **Run by whoever designs a team** — `scaffold` to start one or a role of it from a skeleton, `draft` to draft its roster from the host kit, then, once `check` accepts it, `show` to review a workflow or to ask where an issue is in it, and `rehearse` to try one out.
- **Run by whoever hands the fleet work** — a human or their agent opening decided work. `flows` names the workflow, gives the issue-create line and makes labels. After opening issues, `wake` has the fleet take them up now.
- **Run by whoever sets an agent up** — `skill` prints the skill file that sends their agent to `afkconvoy --help`.
- **Run by a worker** — `gate`, `land`, `verdict`, `intake`, `lock`, `over`, `exclusive`: its prompt names each one as it is needed, and `wake`, above, as its last; `cut` is what a cut's terminal runs, and what you run to go on with a cut that failed. Read them only when you are a worker, or are finding out why one stopped (`rule` is a consult's too).
- **Run by a human an issue waits for** — in a bound repo: `rule` to answer an escalated issue, `send` to put an issue at a stage of your choosing. A `by: human` stage waits for your `verdict`, a worker's command too. [`afkconvoy help humans`](help:humans) says what each case asks of you.
- **Run by a worker's hook** — `guard`, called before each action of a bound repo's worker. Nobody runs it by hand. Its help explains what the worker is refused and why.
- **One transition by hand** — `dispatch`, `close`, `escalate`, `park`, `nudge` and `restart`: each is something a tick does on its own, and `recovery` shows what `dispatch` would continue an issue from. Read one when a plan shows a transition the fleet is not making, or you are told to make it yourself.
- **The claim plumbing** — `scan`, `claim`, `release` and `heartbeat`: what the transitions are built on. Read these only to inspect or repair claims and heartbeats on the remote.

## The topics

Read `afkconvoy help <topic>` when this guide or a command's help names it: it prints that topic, Markdown, as `--help` does.

## Rules to know before you start

- One fleet instance per host per repo. `run` in a second checkout of a repo on the host's checkout list is refused, naming the first: run it there.
- `run` returns once its checkout's first tick ended: the host runner ticks on, in the background, until `afkconvoy stop --all` stops it, keeping the checkout list. `afkconvoy stop` takes one checkout off the list. `tick` is one pass that exits.
- Between ticks a fleet instance sleeps 90 seconds while it has work, or 25 minutes after 3 empty ticks. Commands that change fleet state wake it sooner, including a worker's last `afkconvoy wake`. When a fleet on this host closes an issue or sees it closed, it also wakes every other fleet on the same tracker whose open issues it blocked. That next tick reads GitHub and takes up an issue whose last open blocker closed; its tick log names the closed issue and the fleet instance that saw it. After changing issues with `gh`, run `afkconvoy wake <checkout>` on the fleet's host: `gh` sends no wake.
- Each harness's worker launch command comes from this host's host kit, kept outside the repo. `run` writes it on a host that has none, and `afkconvoy kit` writes it again; neither asks anything. `--worker-command` is gone. A known harness with no entry or command is discovered in the worker login shell, checked, and appended to the latest kit without model probes; an explicit command always wins. A running fleet reads command edits at its next worker launch.
- In a bound repo the worker launch command must end in its harness — Claude Code, pi, Codex, DSH or Kimi Code — taking flags: the fleet adds to it what starts each worker in its role and under the guard ([`afkconvoy help worker-launch`](help:worker-launch) says what, for each harness), and a start refuses a command whose `--help` does not name those flags. Every harness the team could ask for is checked first, and none is ever started in another's place.

## Designing a team, for a bound repo

A bound repo names its team in its config: `team: owner/repo`, or `team: owner/repo/path` for a team in a subdirectory. An issue of it that carries a flow label is walked through that workflow's stages, each performed by a new worker started in the stage's role. A team and a role are each a directory of text files — a whole repo, or a subdirectory of one, so that one repo can hold a team and every role it names — and designing one is editing them. Nothing else holds any of it.

What those files are, and every key of them, is three topics: [`afkconvoy help team`](help:team) (a team's directory and a role's), [`afkconvoy help workflows`](help:workflows), [`afkconvoy help patrols`](help:patrols).

The loop, from nothing:

1. `afkconvoy scaffold team <dir> --role <name> --repo <owner/repo>`: a team's skeleton and, under roles/<name>/, each role's — `--role` once for each — in one repo created on GitHub, with one workflow of one stage, by the first role. For more than one stage — a review, a landing role — read [`afkconvoy help example`](help:example) first: `--example hospital`.
2. `afkconvoy scaffold role <dir>/roles/<name>`: one more role's skeleton, in that checkout: it answers the line to add to team.md. A role several teams share is a repo of its own instead: `--repo`.
3. `afkconvoy check --dir <dir> --team <owner/repo>`: `afkconvoy draft` with the same flags first drafts the roster into team.md. Edit a file, run it, and read the faults: each names its file and key. Repeat until it exits 0. `check` reads a role from GitHub only: a role's edit counts once it is pushed to its default branch.
4. Push the team, name it under `team` in the config of the repo it is to work, and run `afkconvoy check` in that checkout. Then `show` draws each workflow and `rehearse` tries one out.

A role's skill is a file you write ([`afkconvoy help skill-file`](help:skill-file) says its form), or one added with the skills installer you already use, run in the role's directory and committed there. The fleet installs no skill and wraps no installer.

## Usage

```
afkconvoy <COMMAND>
```

## Commands

### Run by the operator

#### `afkconvoy kit`

Write this host's host kit, or enable or disable automatic model casting

##### When to run it

When a harness is installed or removed, a login changes, or its models are to be listed again. Research comes from the watch, through `afkconvoy kit --research <file>`. `run` writes the host kit itself on a host that has none, and a tick writes it again once a day (below). It needs no repo and changes no remote.

##### Who runs it

The operator, or a machine in their place, on the host that starts the workers: it asks nothing, at a terminal or not, and does the same whoever runs it.

##### What it reads and writes

The host kit is $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/afkconvoy/kit.json, or $HOME/.config/afkconvoy/kit.json when XDG_CONFIG_HOME is unset. It is kept on this host and never pushed. It is the only source of worker launch commands. It holds the harnesses this host can start, in order of preference, each with its worker launch command and listed models. Former `stock_consult` kit choices are accepted on read and dropped on write. It is written automatically, with no confirmation:

1. Harnesses. Each known harness whose program `type` finds in an orca terminal — the login shell orca starts, which is the shell a worker gets, with its rc files, PATH and logins — on the command the host kit holds for it, or else its stock worker launch command.
2. Models. Each harness found is asked for the models its own login runs, in an orca terminal. Claude Code is asked through its command with an `initialize` request and no prompt; Codex through its command with `debug models`, its server's list; pi through its command with `--list-models`; Kimi Code through its command with `provider list --json`, under the fleet's isolated home; DSH through `dsh headless`, whose listing plugin asks `https://api.deepseek.com/models` with DSH's account token from `$DSH_HOME/.credentials.yaml` (default `~/.dsh`), or its `DEEPSEEK_API_KEY` when no account token is held. The server's ids and display names are used, never a bundled catalog. This is the sole credential the fleet reads, through DSH's credential service, only for listing: never printed or stored, and sent only to DeepSeek. Not signed in or a server refusal leaves DSH out with the reason.
3. Default first. No model is sent a prompt. A harness found and listed is held at once, each model it newly lists `research pending`, which no worker is started on. A harness with no placed model starts its workers on its own login's default model, with no model flag — Codex too, on its own default. `plan` and `doctor` say so as each harness's `default_model` and `research_pending`.
4. Names. A model's id is exactly the id its harness lists, and a worker is started on it. Its `names` are the names its listing shows it by (Claude Code's `Opus 5.5`) and the aliases research ties to it with a dated source.
5. Order. Established harness and model order is retained, including switches made while listing or research run. New harnesses follow in this fixed order: claude-code, pi, codex, dsh, kimi. New models follow established models; research may rank discoveries without displacing established priority. The first harness and its first placed model are the host kit's first, or its default while none is placed.
6. Research. The watch researches listed identities using its web tools, once across harnesses, and writes a JSON file through `afkconvoy kit --research <file>`. The kit itself calls no model. Unplaced models are a doctor finding: a watch started for other work takes them too; research alone starts one at most once a day. A harness with no placed model stays on its default. Sourced research is kept as good_at, names, sources ({url, date}) and researched_at (epoch seconds), and is never refreshed on a schedule. A caster is told good_at (`afkconvoy cast --help`).

A model named by a roster entry or a `model:` label matches a placed model the host kit holds for its harness when it is its id or one of its names, whatever the case; with the provider prefix left off where that leaves one match (`gpt-6-sol` for pi's `openai-codex/gpt-6-sol`). A name with two matches matches neither, and says which two; one with none says the nearest names.

`afkconvoy kit --cast on` enables automatic model casting on this host; `afkconvoy kit --cast off` disables it. These change only `cast` in an existing kit, send no prompt and leave its refresh time unchanged. Run `afkconvoy kit` first on a host without one. New kits and older kits with no setting default off. Every checkout shares this setting, retained through rebuilding, daily refresh and runner restart. With casting off, workers follow matching model labels or the selected harness's first eligible model; with it on, a caster chooses only among multiple models within selected harnesses (`afkconvoy cast --help`).

Without --cast or --research it says on stderr where the file is, what it holds — each harness's placed models, or its default model, and those `research pending`, `not researched` or settled — and what was left out.

##### What it answers

With --cast: {path, cast, changed}, the kit file, the resulting boolean and whether it changed. With --research: {path, written, placed, settled, kit}, the host kit file, true, each model placed or settled as {harness, model} in its respective array, and the resulting kit. Otherwise {path, written, kit, left_out}: the file; true; the kit written; and each harness or model not kept, as {harness, model, why} — model absent for a whole harness — why `not installed`, `listing failed`, or `no longer listed`. Run twice with nothing changed, it writes the same kit. Errors: orca not running, with the line that starts it; a kit that cannot be read or written.

A harness with `models` [] or no placed model starts on its default. Automatic command discovery can append a harness with no models; one written by hand or by an older release is also read as it is: a model named in it with no research is started on until research answers for it, when the watch supplies its research. Neither the kit nor `left_out` carries probe evidence any more: an older kit's `probed` fields are read and not written again.

##### The research file

Research states: `research pending` is a newly listed model awaiting dated research; `not researched` is an older release's model with no dated answer, also awaiting research. Neither is started on. A settled model has a dated source and a reason research found it unsuited to workers: it is not placed, is named by no unplaced-model finding and starts no watch. The finding names exactly the models awaiting research, including models held with no dated answer; every one can be placed or settled through `afkconvoy kit --research <file>`. Placements and settlements survive routine relisting; an identity dropped from the kit and later listed anew awaits research again.

`afkconvoy kit --research research.json` reads the existing host kit, checks the whole file, and atomically writes the placements and settlements. It needs neither a checkout nor orca. Read `afkconvoy doctor --all` for current ids and names. To place a model, use:

```json
{"models":[{"harness":"claude-code","model":"listed-id","good_at":"wide refactors; slower on small fixes","names":["sourced alias"],"sources":[{"url":"https://vendor.example/model-card","date":"2026-10-26"}]}]}
```

To settle an unsuitable model, replace good_at and names with a nonempty settled reason:

```json
{"models":[{"harness":"codex","model":"codex-auto-review","settled":"approval reviewer, unsuited to workers","sources":[{"url":"https://vendor.example/reviewer","date":"2026-10-26"}]}]}
```

Each entry names an exact listed id of a held harness. Name each identity once across harnesses: the same id without its provider prefix shares research, including settlements. Each entry supplies either nonempty good_at describing coding strengths and weaknesses, with optional nonempty sourced names, or a settled reason with no names. Every entry needs at least one HTTP or HTTPS source URL and its publication or update date as a calendar date YYYY-MM-DD. Use primary and high-trust sources, with live web search. The models array ranks newly placed models, after established model priority; harness priority, commands, cast and existing dated research stay as held. Models omitted stay as held for a later watch.

Refusals name the file and fault and write nothing: malformed JSON, unknown fields, unknown harnesses or ids, repeated identities, conflicting outcomes, empty good_at, settled reason or names, missing or malformed dated sources, or a file answering no model awaiting research. Correct the file and run the command again. The answer lists every placement and settlement, including identities shared by another harness. Research does not change when the models were last listed (`refreshed`).

##### What trips you up

A harness or model left out is gone from the file: commands and research are kept only for what is kept. At a worker launch, a known harness with no command is discovered in the worker's login shell and its checked stock command is merged into the kit, without model probes or research. An explicit command always wins. `--worker-command` is gone: a harness's command is the host kit's. A command is an opaque shell string; an unbound repo starts it under nice with its worktree's TMPDIR, adding its harness's model flag for the model an issue's casting or the host kit's first names, and its harness's worktree-trust setup. Codex also receives a session-private user directory and the effort read from the host user's own Codex config at each launch; no saved worker preference selects either. A bound repo adds its role flags ([`afkconvoy help worker-launch`](help:worker-launch)).

Writing the kit sends no prompt to any listed model. A listed model that fails when its worker starts is found by worker health, classed `model` at model scope and left out; its hourly recovery probe brings it back. A harness refusing every prompt is paused and has its own hourly recovery probe. Those health probes are the only model probes; kit writes, switches and refreshes make none.

##### It stays current

A tick — of `run`, or `afkconvoy tick` — writes the host kit again once its file was last written a day ago or more, before anything else: a newly listed model waits for the watch, and a model no longer listed is dropped. A harness that cannot be found or listed is kept, and a pause leaves it out, as above. The file's modification time is when it was last written — by `kit`, by `run` on a host without one, or by a tick — and `plan` and `doctor` answer it as `host_kit.refreshed`. Every fleet of the host shares the file and the lock beside it (kit.refresh): one of them writes it again, once a day, and the others read what it wrote. A refresh that changed the host kit is a line of the run log, `refresh_kit (fleet): the host kit was written again: added claude-code sonnet; dropped claude-code opus`; one that failed is one too, and is tried again an hour later. The pause is the host's running state, in its cache: this file is not changed. `plan`, `doctor` and the panel say which is paused, since when and why.

##### Usage

```
afkconvoy kit [OPTIONS]
```

##### Arguments

- `--cast <CAST>`: Enable or disable automatic model casting on this host, without probing
  - Values:
    - `on`
    - `off`
- `--research <RESEARCH>`: Place or settle the watch's sourced model research from a checked JSON file

#### `afkconvoy checkouts`

Say which checkouts this host works and how each stands

##### When to run it

To see every repo of this host at once: which checkouts its host runner works, whether each one's fleet instance runs, and whether it has work. A session that looks after every repo of the host asks this — and `afkconvoy doctor --all` for what is wrong with each — instead of keeping a list of its own: the checkout list is the one home of which checkouts there are.

##### Who runs it

The operator, or a session of theirs that looks after every repo of the host: anywhere on this host, since it is about no one checkout.

##### What it reads and writes

The checkout list: checkouts.json in the cache directory (`afkconvoy help cache` says where it is). The host runner, asked on its socket which checkouts it holds a fleet instance of: where none runs, the list alone answers. Each checkout's tick log, for whether its fleet instance is broken and for its last tick, and its entry, for its concurrency and its tracker. It writes nothing, asks neither GitHub nor the remote, and makes no startup probe: it is safe beside a live fleet, as often as you like.

##### What it answers

```json
{"host_runner": {"pid": 4242, "version": "0.6.0", "log": "<cache>/host-runner.log",
                 "panel": "http://127.0.0.1:7070/"},
 "checkouts": [{"checkout": "/Users/me/Developments/hkj", "repo": "github.com/me/hkj",
  "instance": "me-h1-1a2b3c4d", "state": "running", "broken": null,
  "ticked": 1767225600, "idle": false, "holding": 2, "frontier": 1,
  "concurrency": {"in_force": 6, "said_by": "checkout"}, "tracker": "me/issues",
  "tick_log": "<cache>/runs/hkj-0123456789abcdef.jsonl"}]}
```

- `host_runner`: the one running — its pid, its version, its log and where it serves the panel — or null where none runs. `<cache>` stands for the cache directory, whole in the answer.
- `checkouts`: each checkout on the list, in its order; [] with none:

  - `checkout`: its root. `repo`: the repo its remote `origin` names, as `run` answers it; null where it is no git checkout any more
  - `state`: `broken` — its fleet instance is broken (`afkconvoy run --help`), as its tick log says, whether or not a host runner runs to start it again; else `running` — the host runner holds its fleet instance; else `stopped` — no host runner runs, or it holds none of it. `afkconvoy run` in the checkout starts a broken or stopped one at once
  - `broken`: as `afkconvoy doctor` answers it under `fleet`: {why, since, next, instance} — why, as it last broke; since when, and when the host runner starts it again, in epoch seconds, null where no host runner runs; and the fleet instance that broke, "" where none had started. null where it is not broken
  - `instance`: its fleet instance id: the one running, null until its start is logged; else the last one its tick log names, null where it names none
  - `ticked`: when that fleet instance's last tick ended, in epoch seconds; null with none
  - `idle`, `holding`, `frontier`: as that tick ended: whether the fleet instance was idle — it held nothing, nothing of its was on the base branch, and its frontier was empty — the claims it held, and the frontier issues it left undispatched (`afkconvoy tick --help`). null with no tick, or one that failed whole; `idle` null too of a tick logged by an older release
  - `concurrency`: {in_force, said_by}: how many claims its fleet instance holds at work at once on this host, and who says it, as `afkconvoy plan` answers it: `checkout` (`afkconvoy run --concurrency`) or `default`. {error} where its config cannot be read, or it is no git checkout any more
  - `tracker`: the repo its fleet reads and writes its issues in, `<owner>/<repo>`, as its entry says it (`afkconvoy run --tracker`); null where it says none, and the checkout's own repo is its tracker
  - `tick_log`: the file its fleet instance logs its ticks in, as `run` answers it; null where it is no git checkout any more

It exits 0 whatever the checkouts' states. Errors, as {"error": …} with a non-zero exit: the checkout list cannot be read; the host runner cannot say which checkouts it holds — it is of an older afkconvoy, which `afkconvoy run` in any checkout moves onto this one; it ended before it answered; or it answered nothing within 10 seconds.

##### What trips you up

- `idle`, `holding` and `frontier` are of the last tick, not of now: those of a stopped or broken checkout are as its fleet instance last ticked, which `ticked` dates. `afkconvoy doctor`, in the checkout, reads GitHub as it is now.
- A checkout `run` is adding is on no list until its first tick ends, and is not answered until then; one `stop` took off is not answered.
- A broken checkout the host runner starts again is `running` once its tick log keeps that start: it is back once the start's first tick ends, and broken again if it ends before. `afkconvoy doctor` says the same of it.
- `host_runner.panel` is where the host runner serves the panel: the address `afkconvoy panel --open` answers, with no need to ask it. Where no host runner runs it is null, as `host_runner` is whole; where the host runner serves none, it alone is null, and `panel --open` says why. `afkconvoy panel --help` says what the page shows.

##### Usage

```
afkconvoy checkouts
```

#### `afkconvoy config`

Print the repo's config as JSON, defaults filled

##### When to run it

First, before `plan` and `run`: it shows what the fleet goes by in this repo, or why the config cannot be read. Run it again after editing the config.

##### Who runs it

The operator, in a checkout of the repo.

##### What it reads and writes

It reads one file — docs/agents/afkconvoy.md of the checkout it is about, or `--file` — and of that file only the first ```yaml block. It writes nothing, and reads neither GitHub nor the remote.

##### The config file

A markdown file. The keys of its ```yaml block are the keys of the answer below, named and written alike: a file holding every key, each at its default, is

~~~markdown
# afkconvoy config

```yaml
base_branch: "main"                # required: it has no default
gate_command: ./gate.sh            # required: it has no default
gate_seconds: 3600
ready_label: ready-for-agent
epic_labels: [epic, prd]
escalate_label: ready-for-human
lock_label: fleet-lock
team: acme/team                    # naming a team binds the repo
patrols: []
intake_limit: 50
```
~~~

A key left out is at the value shown, so the shortest config is the first two lines, and a bound repo's those and `team`. The last two are read only beside `team`: an unbound repo leaves all three out, and may say one key more, never beside `team`:

```
escalate_to: human                 # legacy consult is accepted; both escalate for the watch
```

What is outside the block is yours to explain it in — but for a second block opened by the line ```yaml cut, which names the repo's cut steps and turns cutting on (`afkconvoy cut --help`). It is read beside this one; older versions read only this one, and refuse nothing for it.

No command writes this file: write it, commit it, and run `afkconvoy config`.

##### What it answers

{"base_branch", "gate_command", "gate_seconds", "ready_label", "epic_labels", "escalate_label", "lock_label"} — every key, the defaults filled in. `gate_seconds` is the gate limit: how many seconds a run of `gate_command` is given, by `afkconvoy gate` and by a landing turn alike, before it is ended and is red (default 3600). It is written nowhere else: neither command has a flag for it. A config that leaves it out is a finding of `afkconvoy doctor`. `lock_label` is the label of a fleet lock (default fleet-lock): while an open issue carries it, the fleet works lock issues only (`afkconvoy lock --help`). How many claims a fleet instance holds at work at once is no key: it is its checkout's, said on the host that works it (`afkconvoy run --concurrency`), and 3 until that host says otherwise. A config that still names `concurrency` is read all the same, but for that key, which changes nothing: `afkconvoy doctor` reports it as `info`, since nothing is held up, with the file and key to delete. Where the checkout says none and the config names a different number than the one in force, its fix first gives the `afkconvoy run` that keeps that number on the host. `afkconvoy plan` says the concurrency in force, and who says it.

A repo whose config names a team is a bound repo, and answers three keys more: {"team", "patrols", "intake_limit"} — the team's directory as owner/repo or owner/repo/path (a whole repo, or a subdirectory of one), which of its patrols run here, by name (default none; `afkconvoy check` holds them against the team's, and `afkconvoy tick --help` says when one runs), how many issues taken in by workers may be open (default 50). A config names no harness: what each worker runs is its team's `roster`'s to say (`afkconvoy help roster`), within what the host kit holds (`afkconvoy kit --help`). A repo that names no team is unbound and answers the seven above and one legacy key: {"escalate_to"}, always `human`. Existing `consult` values still load, but every hand-off escalates for the host's watch to answer. Only a consult explicitly named by a bound repo's stage is asked before escalation (`afkconvoy help humans`).

Where the file names cut steps, the answer has one key more: {"cut": {"set", "publish", "initial"?}} — each as the ```yaml cut block says it. Optional `initial: X.Y.Z` declares the first version to cut when the remote has no version tag; after the first tag it is ignored.

Errors: the file cannot be read; it has no ```yaml block; a ```yaml cut block has a key but `set`, `publish` and `initial`, lacks a required step, a step names nothing to run, or `initial` is not X.Y.Z; `base_branch` or `gate_command` is missing; a key is unknown or of the wrong type; `gate_seconds` is not a whole number from 1; `team` is neither owner/repo nor owner/repo/path; a `harness`, which a config names no more — the error says the line to delete; `patrols` or `intake_limit` is set where no `team` is; `escalate_to` is neither consult nor human, or is set beside `team` — the error names the key. Without `--file`, outside a git checkout: "is not in a git checkout".

##### What trips you up

- It reads the config only. Whether the team it names loads is `afkconvoy check`.
- It reads the file as it is in this checkout, committed or not. A worker reads the one in its own worktree, which is cut from the base branch: a change is in force only once it is on the base branch.

##### Which checkout it is about

Name it after the command, as `[CHECKOUT]`: a checkout of the repo, or any directory in one, which names that checkout. Naming none, it is about the checkout it is run in. It only reads: a worker's worktree is one too.

##### Usage

```
afkconvoy config [OPTIONS] [CHECKOUT]
```

##### Arguments

- `[CHECKOUT]`: The checkout it is about, or a directory in it [default: the one it is run in]
- `--file <FILE>`: The config file [default: docs/agents/afkconvoy.md of this checkout]

#### `afkconvoy check`

Read a team and its workflows: what was read, or every fault

##### When to run it

After every edit to a team's files, a role's skills or a repo's `team` key, and before a fleet is started on a bound repo: it says whether the team loads, and if not, every fault at once. Edit, run it, and repeat until it exits 0.

##### Who runs it

The operator, or whoever designs the team: in a checkout of a bound repo, or anywhere with `--team` or `--dir`.

##### What it reads and writes

It writes nothing but a copy the fleet has not got yet (below). It reads a team's files, and of each role's directory which skills it holds and what each one's `SKILL.md` opens with, which harnesses it holds limits for, and whether a file of it would have a harness load other rules.

What those files are, and every key of each: `afkconvoy help team`, `afkconvoy help workflows` and `afkconvoy help patrols`.

Without a flag it reads the config of this checkout for `team`, and that directory from GitHub at the head of its repo's default branch — and holds the config's `patrols` against the patrols that team has.

`--team owner/repo` or `--team owner/repo/path` names the team instead. `--dir <path>` reads a team's files from a directory as they are, committed or not. Every role is always read from GitHub, at the head of its repo's default branch. A directory says no repo, so a role it names as `./path` is a fault — unless `--team` beside `--dir` says which team on GitHub the files are an edit of: the role is then read from that repo.

A repo on GitHub — the team's, and each role's — is asked for the commit at its head, and read from the fleet's copy of that commit: the one a worker's directory is taken out of, kept read-only under the cache directory (copies/<owner>/<repo>/<commit>): `afkconvoy help cache` says where that directory is on this host, and what moves it.

Only a commit the fleet has no copy of yet is cloned, so a role pushed since the last run is read at its new head, and one that has not moved costs one question. A repo is asked and cloned once however many roles it holds, and a role in the team's own repo is read at the team's commit. The repos are read at once, not one after another.

It reads this host's host kit (`afkconvoy kit --help`) for each role's range, and asks no harness anything: which models a harness knows is the host kit's to hold.

##### What it answers

{"team", "path", "commit", "files", "escalate_label", "rules", "host_user", "dsh_profile", "split", "roles", "workflows", "patrols", "precedents"} — what it read.

`team` is the team's repo and `path` its directory there, "" for a whole repo — with `--dir`, the directory read and null. `commit` is the team's commit read, null with `--dir`; `files` the definition files read, each from the team's directory. `rules` is whether the team has rules of its own: a `CLAUDE.md` in its directory, which every one of its workers is given.

`host_user` is whether its workers are given the host user's own skills and rules beside their role's: true unless the team file says `host_user: false`, and a value that is not true or false is a fault (`afkconvoy help roles`). It is each role's default.

`split` is whether stage briefs offer splitting: true unless the team file says `split: false`. Anything but true or false is a fault (`afkconvoy help team`). `dsh_profile` is `fleet` (default) or `host-user`: which profile DSH workers load, independently of host_user. A role may say its own choice; check answers its effective dsh_profile and refuses every other value.

Each of `roles` is {"name", "repo", "path", "commit", "host_user", "dsh_profile", "skills", "above", "limits", "roster", "range", "left_out", "unmatched", "nothing_safe"}: `path` is the role's directory in `repo`, "" for a whole repo; `commit` the one the role's repo was read at; `host_user` whether its workers are given the host user's skills and rules — its own say, `{ dir, host_user, dsh_profile }`, or the team's; a key of that map but those three, or a `host_user` that is not true or false, is a fault; `above` each `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/` a directory above the role holds in its repo, as a path from the repo's root — but for the team's own `CLAUDE.md`, where the team's directory is above the role: those are the team rules, which a worker is given; `limits` the harnesses the role holds limits for — a hook or a denied permission in its `.claude/settings.json` for claude-code, an entry of its `.pi/extensions/` for pi, a hook in its `.codex/hooks.json` for codex, a `.dsh/cordis.patch.yml` overlay for dsh, a hook or denied permission in its `.kimi-code/limits.toml` for kimi; `roster` its entry in the team's roster, {"cast", "run": [{"harness", "model", "good_at"}]} with null for what it leaves out, and null for a role it names none for; `range` its range on this host, [{"harness", "models"}] in the order a worker takes them — the host kit whole for a role with no entry, or whose entry matches nothing in the host kit, less each harness the role holds no limits for while it holds limits for another, and null where this host has no host kit (`afkconvoy help roster`); `left_out` each harness its entry and the host kit allow it and its range leaves out, [{"harness", "why"}] — why `no limits for pi` — and null where this host has no host kit; `unmatched` what its roster entry allows and the host kit holds, where the entry matches nothing in the host kit — the role then ranges over the host kit whole — and null otherwise; `nothing_safe` why no worker of it can be started on this host, where it holds limits for no harness the host kit holds — its stages wait — and null otherwise. Each of `workflows` is {"name", "flow_label", "max_rework", "max_consecutive_rework", "stages", "land"}, the defaults filled in; each stage is {"name", "by", "do", "writes", "escalate", "pass", "reject"}. `unmatched_models` lists each roster model matching nothing held, as {role, harness, model, holds, said}, with the nearest names or the two matches; a tick opens one issue for each in the team’s repo.

Each of `patrols` is {"name", "by", "do", "every", "max_open", "max_runs_a_day", "max_landed_a_day", "runs_here"}: `every` in seconds, `max_runs_a_day` null where the file says none. `runs_here` is whether the config of this checkout names the patrol — false with `--team` and `--dir`, which read no config. `precedents` is {"by", "do", "max_open"}, or null where the team names nobody to propose them.

A team with a fault: {"error", "faults"} and exit 1. `faults` holds every fault of the team, not the first: each {"file", "key", "problem", "see"}. `key` is a path from the top of the file's yaml, counting from 0 — `stages[1].on.reject` — and empty when the fault is the file itself. `see` is the command that prints the help topic describing that file, to run as it is: `afkconvoy help workflows` for a workflow's, `afkconvoy help patrols` for a patrol's, and `afkconvoy help team` for the team file — a role is named there, and that topic says what its directory holds — and for the config's keys that bind the repo. A fault in a file no topic describes has no `see`.

A fault is one of: an unknown key, or one written twice; a wrong type; a duplicate stage name; a stage named `land`, `done` or `human`; a `pass` or `reject` that names no stage; a `reject` to its own or a later stage; a stage no path from the first reaches; a stage whose passes never come to `land` or `done`; a `pass: land` with no `land:`, or a `land:` no pass leads to; a role the team file does not name; a role named as none of owner/repo, owner/repo/path and ./path; a role's path with a `..`, or an absolute one; a role whose repo cannot be read, or whose path is no directory at its head; a role's directory that is the team's or contains it, or is inside the team's `workflows/` or `patrols/`; a role's directory that contains another role's or is inside one — two names for one directory are none; a symlink in a role in a subdirectory that leaves the role's directory; a file in a role's directory that a harness would load in place of `CLAUDE.md`, its rules under every harness — pi `AGENTS.override.md`, `AGENTS.md` or `AGENTS.MD`, Codex `AGENTS.override.md` or `AGENTS.md` — the fault naming the file and each harness that would load it, whatever harnesses the role may run; a role's limits that cannot be read; a skill its role's directory does not hold; a missing `by`, `do` or `on`; a `harness` or a `model` in a stage or a patrol, which name none any more — the fault says the line to delete and the roster entry to write in its place; in the `roster`, an entry for a name that is no role of the team, a `run` that is missing or empty, a `harness` that names no harness, or an allowance written twice; a flow label two workflows take, or one that is the team's escalate label, the repo's lock label or an epic label — under `label`, or the file where it is the `flow:<name>` it names none in place of; a patrol file whose name is not a patrol's; an `every` that is no duration; a missing `every` or `max_open`; and — in the config, docs/agents/afkconvoy.md, under `patrols` — a name the team has no patrol for.

A team that loads is then held to its harnesses, and these are faults too, each with its file and key, all at once:

- A skill a worker is asked to perform whose file is not in the form every harness reads a skill in: its directory holds no `SKILL.md`, or one that opens with no frontmatter, or whose frontmatter says another `name` than the directory's, or no `description`. The key is the `do` that names the skill — `stages[1].do`, `stages[1].escalate.do`, `land.do`, a patrol's `do`, and `precedents.do` in team.md — and each `do` that names it has the fault. The form is in `afkconvoy help skill-file`. A skill no `do` names is not held to it.
- A roster entry that lets a role run a harness it holds no limits for, while it holds limits for another: the fault names the role and both harnesses, and its key is that `harness` of the entry (`roster.dev.run[1].harness`). A role with no limits at all is no fault. A role the roster names no entry for ranges over the host kit, less what it holds no limits for: that is no fault, and `left_out` names it.

A warning, on stderr, for each workflow whose file says nothing above its yaml block: that prose is what `afkconvoy flows` answers as what the workflow is for, and whoever hands the fleet work chooses a workflow by it. The team loads all the same.

A note, on stderr, for each role with something in `above`: a session opened by hand in the role's directory loads those rules too, and a worker, given the role's directory alone, does not. The team loads all the same, and it exits 0.

A note, on stderr, for each worker on codex whose role holds an `.agents/skills/` or a `.codex/skills/` itself, the skill the worker is asked to perform not in either: Codex finds skills there and not in `.claude/skills/`, the fleet leaves what a role holds there as it is, and the worker would not be shown that skill. A role that holds neither is given a link to its skills, in the fleet's copy, and nothing is noted. The team loads all the same, and it exits 0.

A note, on stderr, for a team whose directory holds a `.claude/`: the hooks and skills there are loaded by no worker. Of a team's directory a worker is given the rules, and a hook and a skill are a role's. The team loads all the same, and it exits 0.

Other errors, as {"error": …}: the repo's config names no team and no flag was given; the config cannot be read, the error naming its file and the key — a `harness` there is one, which a config names no more; the team's repo cannot be read, or the team's path is no directory at its head.

##### What trips you up

- From GitHub it reads what is pushed to the default branch. An edit in a checkout of the team is checked with `--dir`; a role's is checked only once it is pushed, wherever the role is — in the team's own repo too.
- A role's `range` is this host's: run `check` on the host the fleet runs on, after `afkconvoy kit`.
- Only `check` holds a team to its harnesses, and a skill's file to its form: a tick loads the team and starts its workers without asking again.
- Following `pass` alone from any stage must end. A loop back is made with `reject`, which the breakers count; a loop of passes nothing would ever stop.
- A stage nothing leads to is reported only once every `pass` and `reject` names a stage: fix those first and run it again.

##### Which checkout it is about

Name it after the command, as `[CHECKOUT]`: a checkout of the repo, or any directory in one, which names that checkout. Naming none, it is about the checkout it is run in. It only reads: a worker's worktree is one too.

##### Usage

```
afkconvoy check [OPTIONS] [CHECKOUT]
```

##### Arguments

- `[CHECKOUT]`: The checkout it is about, or a directory in it [default: the one it is run in]
- `--team <TEAM>`: The team's directory on GitHub, as owner/repo or owner/repo/path [default: the team this checkout's config names]
- `--dir <DIR>`: A directory of a team's files, read as they are instead of from GitHub; with --team, as an edit of that team: a role it names as ./path is read from that repo

#### `afkconvoy doctor`

Say what the fleet on this host is doing and what is wrong with it, each finding with its fix

##### When to run it

When something looks wrong, and before anything else: a fleet that seems stuck, an issue nobody works, a worker that sits there — or when you are asked "is it working?". Run it before you file a bug, too, and put its answer in the report. It is one command for what `scan`, `takeover --list`, `plan`, `show` and orca each say a part of, and it is the only one that says what is wrong.

With `--all`, for every repo of this host at once: each checkout on the host's checkout list, as `doctor` in it answers. A session that looks after every repo of the host runs it, beside `afkconvoy checkouts`, and keeps no list of its own.

##### Who runs it

The operator, in a checkout of the repo, on the host the fleet runs on. No `--instance` is needed: it finds the fleet instance of this host's `run` itself. With `--all`, anywhere on that host.

##### What it reads and writes

It reads this host (the commands the fleet needs, in a login shell; orca), the log this host's `run` keeps of its ticks, the open issues, PRs and stage records on GitHub, whether GitHub says the tracker is public, the claims, heartbeats and recorded gate runs on the remote, and orca after the worker of each claim. It writes nothing on GitHub and nothing on the remote, and makes no startup probe: it is safe beside a live fleet, as often as you like. It fixes nothing either: each finding names the command that does.

With `--all` it reads the checkout list (checkouts.json in the cache directory) and the same of each checkout on it, all at once.

##### What it answers

{"host", "fleet", "claims", "issues", "waiting_on_human", "proposals", "refusals", "findings"}

- `host`: what this host has of what the fleet needs:

  - `tools`: each command needed — a harness only where a worker launch command the fleet could be asked for runs it by name: {name, state} — state is ready, missing or logged_out; of orca also not_running, knows_no_checkout (the checkout worktrees are cut from was never added to it) or unasked
  - `worker_commands`: the host kit commands and their callers. The first eligible kit harness is selected for each role.
  - `host_kit`: {path, cast, refreshed, harnesses}: where the kit is kept; when it was last written, in epoch seconds — by `kit`, by `run`, or by a tick's daily refresh (`afkconvoy kit --help`); each harness in order, first first, with its full worker launch command, its models in order, each with its good_at or settled reason, sources and researched_at; `default_model` (it has no placed model, so a worker runs its login's default, with no model flag) and `research_pending` (it holds a model awaiting research). {path, error} when unreadable. `afkconvoy kit` writes it again.

    Research states: `research pending` is a newly listed model awaiting dated research; `not researched` is an older release's model with no dated answer, also awaiting research. Neither is started on. A settled model has a dated source and a reason research found it unsuited to workers: it is not placed, is named by no unplaced-model finding and starts no watch. The finding names exactly the models awaiting research, including models held with no dated answer; every one can be placed or settled through `afkconvoy kit --research <file>`. Placements and settlements survive routine relisting; an identity dropped from the kit and later listed anew awaits research again.

    A harness with `models` [] or no placed model runs on its default model with no model flag, and is no fault. Automatic command discovery, a switch, failed research or a hand-written kit can leave one. `afkconvoy kit` lists them; the watch supplies research through `afkconvoy kit --research <file>`. A tick lists an empty Codex entry without waiting for the daily refresh, with an hour between unsuccessful tries. A roster or casting model that matches nothing placed is still reported as such.
  - `settings`: the host settings (`afkconvoy run --help`): {file, said, in_force} — each by its key, the name of the flag of `run` that names it (`hot_cores` for `--hot-cores`), in that flag's units: said is what the host says, null where it says none and the default holds; in_force what holds for this repo's fleet on this host, each default worked out for it — the panel's port 7070 where the host says none. {file, error} where the file cannot be read
  - `admission`: whether a tick would start a new worker on this host now, the thresholds in force and what the host reads: as `plan` answers it (`afkconvoy plan --help`), or {error} where a share the host says is wrong. A tick that admission held back is no "started no worker" finding.
  - `exclusive`: the host's queues as {lanes: {worker, repos}, running, waiting}. Each lane has {running, running_all, waiting}, where running is the first active command for older readers and running_all lists every active command; repos lists {repo, queue} for light gates. The top-level running and waiting are the worker lane for older readers — running is the command that runs alone now, null with none; waiting, those that wait their turn, next first; both empty with no host runner. Each is {command, dir, issue, pid, asked, ran}: the worktree it was run in, the issue of its worker, and when it asked and began to run, in epoch seconds. {error} when the host runner cannot say it
  - `resources`: resource episodes observed by the host runner, with stable ids, active conditions, since, episode, worker or host readings and evidence. Admission and pressure retain their identities during five minutes of recovery. Resource findings also have watch_id, the episode identity that starts at most one watch.
  - `watch`: this host's watch (`afkconvoy run --help`, WATCH): {directory, stock, running, last, unavailable} — directory is where the next watch runs, stock whether it uses afkconvoy's own instruction; running and last are each {id, directory, stock, items, started, harness, model, terminal, transcript, did, attempts, ended, outcome}: why it started (items, each {id, reason}), its session's harness, model and terminal, the file its session prints to, what its sessions printed (did), including each request left with a human, each session whose harness gave out ({harness, model, terminal, why, did}), and how it ended — outcome `ended`, `closed` (its terminal closed before its harness exited), `time_limit` or `no_harness`; null with none. unavailable: why the last watch a look called for could not start or go on, null where it could
  - `installed`: the release installed where the host runner was started from, where the host runner moves onto it or did not: {path, version, from, since, wait_expired, held_back, failed} — the file; the release it says, null where it says none; the host runner's own release; when that file answered, in epoch seconds; whether the 600s wait expired; what holds the move back, each in words ("/Users/me/Developments/hkj is in a tick", "1 exclusive command(s) running"), [] once nothing does, or the last blockers when the wait expired; and why the move failed — it did not start, or does not say its version — null until one did. null with none: nothing newer is installed there, or no host runner runs (`afkconvoy run --help`)
- `fleet`: the `run` of this host for this repo:

  - `alive`: whether one is running now: this host's runner, asked on its socket naming this checkout, holds a fleet instance of this repo
  - `instance`, `host`: its fleet instance id: the one its log names, else the one the claims stamped with this host name; null when this host never ran one
  - `heartbeat_age`: seconds since its heartbeat; null: it has none
  - `heartbeats`: {found, live}: how many heartbeats the remote has, whoever stamped them, and the instance ids of those within the lease. A `run` told to stop removes its own, and a start removes the dead ones that hold nothing: more than one found and not live is fleets nobody started again
  - `log`: the file its ticks are logged in, or "no log": no `run` of this version ran here
  - `last_tick`: {count, ended, next_due, line, did, error}: when its last tick ended and the next is due, in epoch seconds, the line `run` printed, and what `tick` answers as `did`; error, when the tick failed whole. null with no log
  - `failed_steps`: the last 10 failures, newest first: {tick, ended, do, issue, patrol, error, count}. One cause that stopped several steps of a tick is one failure: count is how many, and do, issue and patrol the first's
  - `host_sleep`: {checked, slept, kept_awake_by}: its last check for host sleep — when it ended, whether it put the host to sleep, and else what kept the host awake, each in words: "the host's local time is outside its sleep hours, 00:00-06:00" among them. null: it made none, the host settings keeping the host awake, or never idle 10 minutes
  - `events`: the last 20 events that reached a `run` of this host, newest first, whichever instance: {at, event, cause, instance} — event being wake (between ticks, or during one), start, stop (told to, by SIGTERM or SIGINT), broken, back, moved or not_moved (the host runner moved onto a newer afkconvoy, with both releases, or that one did not start: `afkconvoy run --help`), host_sleep, host_wake, watch (a thing a watch did, and how it ended: `afkconvoy run --help`) or cut (a cut started, and how it ended: `afkconvoy cut --help`); cause says what caused it, in words. [] with no log
  - `broken`: {why, since, next, instance}: its fleet instance is broken (`afkconvoy run --help`) — why, as it last broke; since when, and when the host runner starts it again, in epoch seconds, null where no host runner runs on this host; and the fleet instance that broke, "" where none had started. null: it is not broken
  - `concurrency`: {in_force, said_by}: how many claims its fleet instance holds at work at once on this host, as `plan` says it — said_by `checkout` or `default`. {error} where the config or the checkout list cannot be read
  - `tracker`: the repo its fleet reads and writes its issues in, as `afkconvoy checkouts` says it: null where the checkout says none, and its own repo is its tracker. {error} where the checkout list cannot be read
- `claims`: each claim of that instance: {issue, title, status, pr, stage, role, held_for, worker, worktree, gate} — status as `plan` gives it; stage and role in a bound repo; held_for in seconds; worker is {state, quiet}, state being busy, stopped or gone, and null when orca could not say; gate is {green_at} when a green gate run is on record for the tree the worktree is at, else null
- `issues`: as `plan` answers them: {frontier, excluded, escalating, locks, free_slots, patrols} — what a worker can be started on, what waits and why, and what is being handed to a human and why. null when they could not be read
- `refusals`: issue number → the harnesses that refused that task, each with `harness` and `evidence`, read from GitHub. Later starts skip them across every stage; the harness stays healthy for other issues.
- `codex_workers`: this checkout's Codex sessions, each with issue, worktree, harness, model, effort, model_source, effort_source and codex_home (its private session directory). The fleet selects the model (`fleet_selection`), or none while the host kit places no Codex model — model null, Codex's own default (`codex_default`); every start reads the effort from your own ~/.codex/config.toml, or uses Codex's model default. Sources stay attached to the session after your config changes; a saved /model choice is shown with its session's private config as the source. [`afkconvoy help worker-launch`](help:worker-launch).
- `waiting_on_human`: as `plan` answers it, and as the panel lists it under "With a human": every open issue nobody holds that waits for a human — escalated, at a stage that is a human's, past the end of its workflow and still open, or reporting a patrol's failed run — each as {issue, title, why, url, since, answer}: `why` is what kind of wait, then the reason the issue’s comment gives, in its first sentence; `url` is that comment (the report itself for an older failed patrol or cut with no reason comment), or null where no comment explains the wait; `answer` is the line that answers it, to run as it is but for what stands between < and >. An escalation with no position gets the team's only flow label filled in; with several workflows, `why` lists the flow labels to choose `<flow label>` from. null when the issues could not be read
- `proposals`: a bound repo's team's open proposals, including those whose source issue is closed: {team, tracker, max_open, open}. team is the team's repo; tracker names another tracker, null where the checkout's own repo holds the rulings; max_open is the team's limit, null where it names nobody who proposes. `proposals.open` lists each PR from the team's own branches, lowest PR first: {pr, issue, comment, since, age, merge, close} — the PR number, the source issue and the id of its ruling's comment, when the PR opened in epoch seconds and its age in seconds (both null where GitHub said no time), and the exact `gh pr merge <pr> --repo <team>` and `gh pr close <pr> --repo <team>` commands. [] with none; proposals is null in an unbound repo or when the team or fleet state cannot be read. The panel shows these under "With a human" too. Once open proposals reach max_open, a warning finding names the PRs and a merge command: further proposals wait at `full` (`afkconvoy help humans`)
- `findings`: what is wrong, most severe first — none: []. Each is {severity, what, evidence, fix, see}:

  - `severity`: how much it matters, one of those below
  - `what`: the fault, in a sentence
  - `evidence`: what was read that says so
  - `fix`: one command line to run as it is but for what stands between < and > — or, for a fault in a team's or a role's file, or a key the repo's config leaves out, `<file>: <key>` to edit. For an escalation with no position and several workflows, `what` lists the flow labels to choose `<flow label>` from
  - `see`: the command that prints the help topic explaining it: `afkconvoy help humans` where what it reports waits for a human, else `afkconvoy help troubleshooting`, which has a row for each finding

A finding's `severity` is one of, most first:

- `critical`: The fleet does not work, or will not, until it is fixed.
- `warning`: One issue or one patrol is held up, or is about to be.
- `info`: Nothing is held up: said so that a surprise is explained.

It exits 0 with no critical finding, and non-zero with one — printing the same object, not {"error"} — so that a script can gate on it. Errors: "is not in a git checkout". Whatever else cannot be read is itself a finding.

With `--all`:

{"host": {"host_kit", "exclusive", "watch", "resources", "installed"}, "findings", "checkouts": [{"checkout", "repo", "doctor"}], "until"}

- `host`: what of `host` is the host's alone, as above, said once
- `findings`: the host's findings, said once however many checkouts found them, most severe first: a command missing or logged out, orca not running, a harness paused, the host runner not moved onto a newer afkconvoy
- `checkouts`: each checkout on the list, in its order — [] with none — with the repo its remote `origin` names, null where it is no git checkout any more, and its `doctor`: what `doctor` answers in it — `waiting_on_human` and `proposals` among it — but for the host's, which are above. Each is asked as the fleet of the host its `run` named, unless `--host` names one. {"error", "see"} where it could not be asked
- `until`: this look's boundary in epoch seconds, captured before reading any checkout. Pass it as the next `--since`. Null when a checkout or its interval could not be read: keep the previous boundary and try again.

With `--all --since <time>`, each checkout's `doctor.watching` adds what happened on this host and on GitHub. Time is epoch seconds or UTC `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ`. The interval includes `since` and excludes `until`: events stamped in the current second are left for the next look, so adjacent looks lose no step and repeat none. Without `--since`, no interval is read and the state and findings are answered as usual.

- `since`, `until`: the interval's boundaries, in epoch seconds.
- `issues`: each issue that moved, and each issue with an open PR, as {issue, title, pr, steps, last_step}. `steps` are oldest first, each {at, source, step, detail}; source is tick_log or github. Exclusive queue counts, waits, exit codes and run times are in detail, as logged. `last_step` adds `ago`, seconds since the last step, including a step before `since`; null if neither source has one. A queued, running or red gate therefore explains a PR quiet on GitHub.
- `ticks`: ticks that acted, held admission back or failed, oldest first, as {instance, first, last, count, line, failed, did, errors}. Consecutive successful ticks with the same line, steps and errors are folded, count saying how many; every failed tick is separate, including a failure said only in its line.
- `events`: other tick log lines, oldest first, as {at, instance, line}: commands, starts, stops, hot workers and what watches did among them. A command that names no issue stays here.
- `ended`: GitHub's issue_closed, pr_merged, pr_closed and intake steps in the interval, each {at, issue, pr, step, detail}. Fork PRs and another repo's issues in a shared tracker are left out.
- `log`: {file, first, retained_only}: the local log, its oldest retained timestamp (null with none), and true because older lines may have been cut back. The interval can only report local steps still retained. GitHub reads include closed issues and PRs, and their intake and stage records. {error, see} in place of watching means that interval could not be read; the top-level until is null and the command exits non-zero.

It exits non-zero where any finding is critical, the host's or a checkout's, or a checkout could not be asked — printing the same object. Errors: the checkout list cannot be read.

The findings: a command the fleet needs is missing or logged out; orca cannot be asked, or does not know the checkout; the worker launch command of a harness the fleet could be asked for cannot start a worker — said with the harness and what calls for it; no `run` is alive and claims are held; the fleet instance of this checkout is broken — with why, since when and when the host runner starts it again; the same step failed in each of the last three ticks; the team has a fault at its head; a fleet lock stands on an issue that cannot be worked (all critical) — a step failed and has not recovered, including a worker that failed to start, with its error and the line to try again; a claim has no worker; a worker has been stopped for half an hour with its claim still at work; the frontier is not empty, slots are free and the last tick started nobody; a flow label names no workflow of the team; an issue has been at a stage longer than any before it took; an issue is one rework from a breaker; a patrol is failed or full; an issue has waited for a human for more than an hour, its `fix` being the line that answers it; the gate is slow — with the host, the gate limit and the 5 runs, each a commit and its seconds, as `afkconvoy plan` has them, and the issue open for it when there is one; the host runner did not move onto the newer release installed where it was started from — it did not start, does not say its version, or waited past the release move limit — with the file, both releases and why, its `fix` that file's `--version` (all warning) — the repo's config names `concurrency`, which nothing reads any more — with the value it names and the concurrency in force: nothing is held up, even where the values differ. Its `fix` is deleting the key alone where the checkout says its own or the config names the number already in force; otherwise `afkconvoy run <checkout> --concurrency <value>` keeps the config's number on this host before deleting the key; the role or the team a stage in flight started under has moved since; and the repo's config declares no gate limit, so the gate has the default's 3600 seconds before anything ends it: `fix` is the file and the key, `gate_seconds`; and a worktree on this host is kept with no claim on its issue — said with what it holds that the remote does not (uncommitted changes, commits only it has, or nothing), its `fix` the line that removes it, pushing first whatever only it holds (all info).

Moved: the role's directory holds something else at the head of its repo than at the commit the stage started under — a file added, removed or changed. A new commit is not it: in a repo of several roles a push gives every role a new commit, and moves the ones whose directory it changed. The team has moved when its directory has, without what a worker is not given of it: the directories of its roles, and the .claude/ at its top. So a push that changes only a role moves no team, one that changes only the team's rules — the CLAUDE.md at its top, which every worker is given — moves the team, and one that changes a workflow moves no role. A role in a repo of its own moves with every push that changes a file there. The two are compared in the copies this host keeps (copies/ under the cache directory); where the one the stage started under is no longer there, a different commit is all there is to go by, and it is said to have moved. `evidence` gives both commits.

##### What trips you up

- A warning may be the fleet mid-step: a claim has no worker between the tick that took it and the one that starts its worker. Run it again after a tick before you act on one; a critical finding does not go away by waiting.
- It says nothing of ticks nobody logged. A `run` logs under your cache directory (`afkconvoy help cache` says where it is) on the host it runs on: run `doctor` there, as the same user. The log is a log: nothing reads it to decide anything, and deleting it loses only what `doctor` could say of the ticks before.
- It makes no startup probe, so it looks for the fleet's refs where this repo's last `plan`, `tick` or `run` found the remote keeps them. In a clone none ever ran in, it looks under refs/convoy/.
- `fix` is the first thing to try, not a promise: read `afkconvoy <command> --help` of the command it names before you run it.

##### Worker proxy bypass

`--worker-no-proxy [HARNESS=]HOSTS` shows what a start with those flags would give each harness, under `worker_no_proxy`: [`afkconvoy help worker-proxy`](help:worker-proxy).

##### Which checkout it is about

Name it after the command, as `[CHECKOUT]`: a checkout of the repo, or any directory in one, which names that checkout. Naming none, it is about the checkout it is run in. A worker runs it in its own worktree.

##### Usage

```
afkconvoy doctor [OPTIONS] [CHECKOUT]
```

##### Arguments

- `[CHECKOUT]`: The checkout it is about, or a directory in it [default: the one it is run in]
- `--all`: Every checkout on this host's checkout list, saying the host's findings once
- `--since <SINCE>`: Add what happened since this time (epoch seconds or YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ); requires --all
- `--worker-no-proxy <[HARNESS=]HOSTS>`: Hosts reached directly, comma-separated, for the default harness or HARNESS; repeat for each harness. DSH defaults to api.deepseek.com. An empty list disables the stock addition. Extends no_proxy and NO_PROXY
- `--host <HOST>`: The host whose fleet is asked after [default: this machine's name]

#### `afkconvoy plan`

Show what a tick would act on, changing no fleet state (may push and delete a startup probe; read-only: `afkconvoy doctor`)

##### When to run it

Before `run`, to see what the fleet would start on; and beside a running fleet, to see where every claim stands and why an issue is not on the frontier.

##### Who runs it

The operator, in a checkout of the repo.

##### What it reads and writes

It makes the startup probe — which checks, as a start does, the worker launch command a `run` started now would give every harness the fleet could be asked for (`afkconvoy run --help`) — then the rebuild: the open issues and PRs on GitHub, the claims and heartbeats on the remote, and their landing turns. It changes nothing on GitHub. On the remote it pushes its startup probe and deletes it again, together with what the probe sweeps: a probe an earlier start left behind, and recorded gate runs too old for a landing to believe.

WHEN IT PROBES. Not every time: a startup probe that passed on this host in the last hour stands, and `plan` then makes none — it says so on stderr, repeats that probe's warnings, and pushes nothing. It probes when no probe stands: none passed on this host within the hour — `run` makes one at every start, `tick` and `plan` when they find none — or the config's `base_branch` or `team` changed since, or the remote's URL did, or the note of where the remote keeps the fleet's refs — or no check that found the tracker the checkout says now private stands: one stands for the hour, of that tracker alone. The probe is noted in the repo's git dir (`convoy-probe`), and the check of the tracker beside it (`convoy-tracker`); delete either file to have the next `plan` probe.

The rebuild asks GitHub twice, side by side with one listing of the remote, however many issues are open: one query for the open issues with their comments (an issue with more than a hundred comments is asked about once more), one for the open PRs. In a tracker another repo than the checkout's, GitHub answers only the open issues that carry this repo's repo label, so it asks as often however many repos' issues the tracker holds. It asks once more — for the issues that carry the label `slow-gate` — only while the recorded gate runs of the base branch's landings say the gate is slow.

##### What it answers

{"frontier", "excluded", "waiting_on_human", "mine", "peer_live", "stale", "stale_closed", "free_slots", "now", "locks", "concurrency", "tracker", "admission", "host_kit", "worker_no_proxy"} — "held_back" while admission holds; and in a bound repo "intake", "left_out", "unmatched" and "nothing_safe" where they name some, "patrols" where it names some, and "proposals" while a ruling is proposed as a precedent or waits to be; and "slow_gate" while the gate is slow; and "caster" while one runs or is due; and "cut" in a repo that turns cutting on, or while a cut is going or on the base branch

- `host_kit`: {path, refreshed, harnesses}: this host's kit file; cast, whether this host enables automatic model casting (false by default); when it was last written, in epoch seconds — by `kit`, by `run`, or by a tick's daily refresh (`afkconvoy kit --help`); each harness in order of preference as {harness, command, models, default_model, research_pending}, each model {model, names, good_at, settled, sources, researched_at}. `default_model` is true when the harness has no placed model, so a worker runs its login's default with no model flag; `research_pending` is true while it holds a model awaiting research. good_at is what a caster is told, or a research marker; settled is a reason research found it unsuitable. The research states are defined in `afkconvoy kit --help`. sources holds dated URLs and researched_at the research time, absent where none succeeded. With an unreadable kit, {path, error}. `afkconvoy kit` writes it again.
- `frontier`: issues due to dispatch, with their stage and cast {harness, model, why}. Harness priority is kit order within role eligibility; model labels only match within the selected harness. `selection` lists kit order, eligible candidates, skipped candidates and health evidence.
- `codex_workers`: started Codex sessions with their actual model, effort and sources, as `doctor` answers them. A frontier issue whose cast runs Codex also has `codex`: its next-launch model (null: Codex's own default) and the effort read now from your own ~/.codex/config.toml (`codex_default` with no setting). Existing sessions keep their launch evidence or their own saved /model choice. [`afkconvoy help worker-launch`](help:worker-launch).
- `excluded`: every other open issue, with why: {number, title, reason}. An escalated issue says so — "escalated: waits for a ruling" — and not that it lacks the label its escalation took off. A name that matches nothing never excludes an issue: it runs the default, `unmatched` on the frontier. A bound repo's issue at a stage whose role has no harness on this host it holds limits for waits, "<role> has no harness on this host it holds limits for: ", naming what the role holds limits for and what the host kit holds, and is dispatched once the host kit holds one; one that waits for the caster is "held for the caster: "
- `left_out`: in a bound repo whose team and host kit can be read: each role, in the team's order, with what its range on this host leaves out: {role, left_out: [{harness, why}]} — a harness its roster entry and the host kit allow it and it holds no limits for, while it holds limits for another, why `no limits for pi` (`afkconvoy help roster`)
- `unmatched`: in a bound repo, where some role's roster entry matches nothing in the host kit: {role, why} — the role ranges over the host kit whole, less what it holds no limits for
- `nothing_safe`: in a bound repo, where some role has no harness on this host it holds limits for: {role, why} — its stages wait, and every other stage goes on
- `unmatched_models`: each roster model matching nothing held, {role, harness, model, holds, said}, with the nearest names or the two matches
- `casting`: each open issue, {number, needed, why, stages, running}. why explains the host setting, human labels, a missing model choice or existing matching labels. stages lists {stage, harness, model, followed, why, skipped}; followed says whether a model: label selected the model, skipped explains earlier models. running is {harness, model} recorded at the existing worker's launch, or null. Doctor answers the same under issues.casting, and the panel shows it under Model selection.
- `caster`: while a caster runs or one is due:

  {running_since, due, held, to_cast} — when the one that runs was started (null: none runs), whether a tick starts one now, the frontier's issues held back for it, and every issue a caster started now is given. An uncast issue with a choice to make waits for one, for ten minutes at most from its start: `afkconvoy cast --help`
- `waiting_on_human`: every open issue nobody holds that waits for a human, lowest number first: {issue, title, why, url, since, answer} — `why`: what kind of wait, then the reason the issue’s comment gives, in its first sentence; `url`: that comment (the report itself for an older failed patrol or cut with no reason comment), or null where no comment explains the wait; since when in epoch seconds where GitHub said, and the line that answers it, to run as it is but for what stands between < and >. An escalation with no position gets the team's only flow label filled in; with several workflows, `why` lists the flow labels to choose `<flow label>` from. They are: an escalated issue, one whose records call for a human, one at a stage that is a human's, one whose workflow ended and that is still open, and the report of a patrol's failed run
- `escalating`: in a bound repo, when there are any: the unclaimed issues a tick hands to a human, with why: {number, title, reason}
