- `mine`: the claims of `--instance`: {number, title, status, pr, declared} — `declared` is true while a verdict declared under the claim waits to be acted on: the claim takes no slot meanwhile. In a bound repo with `due`, the stage a worker is to be started on once the claim's stage has declared, where a role performs one. status is one of those below
- `peer_live`: other instances' claims within the lease — never touched
- `stale`: other instances' claims past the lease, on open issues — a tick takes them
- `stale_closed`: the same on closed issues — a tick deletes them (each of the three: {number, instance, sha})
- `free_slots`: how many more claims the instance may take
- `concurrency`: {in_force, said_by}: how many claims the fleet of this checkout holds at work at once on this host — what `free_slots` counts from, beside the claims a fleet lock leaves alone and those whose worker declared — and who says it: `checkout`, where `afkconvoy run --concurrency` said it of this checkout, which keeps it on the checkout list; `default`, where it said none (3). The repo config says none: a `concurrency` it names is read no more
- `tracker`: the repo the fleet of this checkout reads and writes its issues in, `<owner>/<repo>`, where `afkconvoy run --tracker` said one of it, which keeps it on the checkout list; null where it said none, and the checkout's own repo is its tracker. With one, the frontier, `excluded` and every other issue here are the open issues there that carry this repo's repo label, `repo:<owner>/<repo>`; one that carries the repo label of another repo too is excluded, "repo labels of more than one repo" (`docs/adr/0027`)
- `now`: the time the plan was made at, in epoch seconds
- `locks`: the fleet locks standing: the open issues that carry the lock label, lowest number first — none: []. While there is one, the frontier holds lock issues only, and every issue a tick would otherwise dispatch or hand to a human is under `excluded` with the reason "a fleet lock stands (#n)"
- `admission`: whether a tick would start a new worker on this host now (`afkconvoy run --help`, ADMISSION): {admits, held_back_by, shares, thresholds, reading}. held_back_by is each threshold the host is past, as a tick's line says it: none, and it admits. shares are the percentages in force — load_percent_of_cores, memory_free_percent, disk_free_percent — and said_by_host the host settings that said one, by key (admit_load, admit_memory, admit_disk, admit_inspect_after); thresholds what they come to on this host — load, memory_free_percent, disk_free_bytes; reading what the host reads now — cores, load, memory_free_percent, disk_free_bytes, disk_size_bytes, each null where it could not be read
- `worker_no_proxy`: every harness, with {harness, addition, no_proxy, NO_PROXY}: the host list added and the resulting login shell values, with this command's --worker-no-proxy flags. A null addition leaves the inherited spellings alone
- `held_back`: while admission holds: each threshold the host is past, as data: {by: "load", load, limit} in hundredths, {by: "memory", free, floor} in percent, {by: "disk", free, floor} in bytes. The frontier is still what a tick would dispatch once it admits
- `intake`: in a bound repo: {"open", "limit"} — the open issues taken in by workers, counted from their intake records, against the repo's `intake_limit`. With `open` at `limit`, `afkconvoy intake` refuses. An issue a human labelled is not among them
- `patrols`: in a bound repo that names patrols: each, in the order the config names them: {name, standing, every, last_run, open, max_open} — `every` in seconds, `last_run` when its last recorded run started (null: it never ran), `open` the open issues it opened. A patrol whose file says `max_runs_a_day` has it too, and `runs_in_day`: how many of its runs started in the last 24 hours. A patrol with `max_landed_a_day` reports it and `landed_in_day`: the issues it opened that closed as completed in the last rolling 24 hours. One a human asked to run now (`afkconvoy patrol-now --help`) has `asked`: when the ask was made, until a tick starts the run. standing says what a tick does about it:

  - `due`: its interval has passed, or a human asked for it: a tick runs it
  - `not_due`: its interval has not passed since `last_run`
  - `spent`: `runs_in_day` has reached `max_runs_a_day`: it is held until `until` — when the oldest of those runs is 24 hours old
  - `landed`: `landed_in_day` reached `max_landed_a_day`: held until `until`, when enough completions are 24 hours old to fall below the bound. A human's ask respects this bound too
  - `locked`: a fleet lock stands: no patrol runs
  - `full`: `open` has reached `max_open`
  - `failed`: its last run failed, and the issue that reports it — `failure`, in this case only — is still open
  - `running`: a run of `--instance` is still going
  - `peer_running`: a live peer's run is still going
  - `stale_run`: the run is claimed by a peer presumed dead: a tick deletes that claim
- `proposals`: in a bound repo whose team names who proposes precedents: each ruling of a human that is being proposed, or is still to be: {issue, comment, standing} — the issue ruled on and the id of the comment that is the ruling. standing says what a tick does about it:

  - `due`: a tick starts its worker, once the frontier is served
  - `full`: the open proposals on the team's repo have reached the team's `max_open`
  - `locked`: a fleet lock stands: nothing is proposed
  - `running`: its worker, started by `--instance`, may still be at it
  - `peer_running`: a live peer started its worker
  - `stale_run`: it is claimed by a peer presumed dead: a tick ends it
- `cut`: in a repo that turns cutting on (`afkconvoy cut --help`): {standing, newest_tag, initial, past, failure} — `newest_tag` the newest version tag on the remote (none: it has none), `initial` the declared first version, present only without a version tag, `past` how many commits the base branch holds past its newest tag (0 without one), `failure` the open issue that says the last cut failed. standing says what a tick does about it:

  - `due`: the base branch holds commits past `newest_tag`, or the remote has no version tag and `initial` is declared: the next tick that ends idle starts a cut — it holds no claim, nothing is on the base branch, its frontier is empty and admission holds nothing back
  - `tagged`: the base branch holds nothing past `newest_tag`: nothing to cut
  - `untagged`: the remote has no version tag and the repo declares no `initial` version: nothing is cut
  - `failed`: the last cut failed, and `failure` is still open: no cut starts until it is closed
  - `locked`: a fleet lock stands: no cut starts
  - `running`: a cut `--instance` started is still going
  - `peer_running`: a live peer's cut is still going
  - `stale_run`: it is claimed by a peer presumed dead: a tick deletes that claim
  - `off`: the repo turns cutting off, and a cut started before it did is on the base branch
- `slow_gate`: while the gate is slow: {gate_seconds, host, runs, issue}. On `host`, the last 5 landings on the base branch that have a recorded run of the config's `gate_command` with a time all took more than 80% of the gate limit, `gate_seconds`. runs are those 5, newest first: {commit, seconds}. issue is the open issue that says so — the lowest open one carrying the label `slow-gate` — or null: a tick opens one (`afkconvoy tick --help`)

A claim's `status`, under `mine`, is one of:

- `no_pr`: No open PR closes the issue: its worker is still at it, or stopped.
- `landing`: An open PR closes it, and that PR is not on the base branch yet. In a bound repo, only under a landing worker's claim.
- `landed`: Its turn put the work on the base branch, and the landing was cut short before the issue was closed: a tick closes it, then settles the claim.
- `closed`: The issue is closed: a tick settles the claim and releases it.
- `gone`: GitHub says the issue was deleted, or transferred to another repo: nothing is left to settle, and the claim is let go.
- `at_stage`: In a bound repo, a claim on an open issue that is not a landing worker's, whatever PR is open: it was dispatched to a stage, and what that stage declares ends it.

The probe's warnings go to stderr. Errors: a command the fleet needs is missing or logged out, or orca is not running or does not know this checkout (the error names each, with the line to run; `claude` is among them when no custom provider is set, as `run` would then start its workers with it); the repo fails the startup probe (the remote has no base branch, its protection refuses the fleet's push, its tracker is public — the error names it, with the line that says a private one — or the remote takes none of the fleet's refs); the config cannot be read; GitHub or the remote cannot be read.

##### What trips you up

- Without `--instance` nobody's claims are its own: `mine` is empty, a running fleet's claims show under `peer_live`, and `free_slots` is the whole concurrency. To see a running fleet as it sees itself, pass its instance id — `takeover --list` shows every id the remote remembers.
- A lock that stands is not thereby worked. A lock issue is on the frontier only when it would be without the lock: with the ready label in an unbound repo, a flow label in a bound one, no epic label, no open blocker, no claim. `excluded` says which of these keeps it off — and the lock stands until the issue is closed.
- `frontier` is what the rebuild read, and `plan` reads nothing more. An issue that gains an open blocker after it is still listed; a tick reads each issue's blockers once more just before it claims it, and skips the issue then.
- A patrol is due or it is not: one that missed ten intervals runs once. And a run still going takes one slot of the concurrency, like a claim on an issue.
- With a lock standing, `free_slots` counts as free the slot of every claim of `--instance` the lock leaves alone: a lock issue does not wait for them.
- `free_slots` counts as free the slot of every claim of `--instance` that is `declared`: `mine` may hold more claims than the concurrency, and the frontier does not wait out the grace period of a worker that already declared.
- Fleet state is unchanged. When it probes it still pushes to the remote, and deletes there: it needs push access, and it is not a read-only command. To read without writing anything, run `afkconvoy doctor`.
- A slow gate is read off the recorded gate runs the remote still has: a record is swept a day after its run, a landing with no record or with a record that states no time is passed over, and 5 landings spread over hosts none of which has 5 say nothing. After an issue for a slow gate closed, only the landings made since count.
- A probe that stands is trusted, not checked: a command uninstalled or logged out since, or a rule the remote gained, shows as the error of whatever runs into it — or, for the ref layout, not until the next probe. `run` probes at every start.

##### Worker proxy bypass

`--worker-no-proxy [HARNESS=]HOSTS` shows what a start with those flags would give each harness, under `worker_no_proxy`: [`afkconvoy help worker-proxy`](help:worker-proxy).

##### Which checkout it is about

Name it after the command, as `[CHECKOUT]`: a checkout of the repo, or any directory in one, which names that checkout. Naming none, it is about the checkout it is run in. A worker runs it in its own worktree.

##### Usage

```
afkconvoy plan [OPTIONS] [CHECKOUT]
```

##### Arguments

- `[CHECKOUT]`: The checkout it is about, or a directory in it [default: the one it is run in]
- `--worker-no-proxy <[HARNESS=]HOSTS>`: Hosts reached directly, comma-separated, for the default harness or HARNESS; repeat for each harness. DSH defaults to api.deepseek.com. An empty list disables the stock addition. Extends no_proxy and NO_PROXY
- `--instance <INSTANCE>`: The fleet instance whose claims are its own [default: nobody's]

#### `afkconvoy run`

Add a checkout to this host's checkout list, start the host runner where none runs, and answer the checkout's first tick

##### When to run it

To have a repo worked: after `config` answers and `plan` shows the frontier you expect. Run it again after the host runner was stopped or killed, or the host restarted: it starts every checkout on the list, each where its fleet instance left off. An upgrade of afkconvoy (`brew upgrade afkconvoy`) needs none: the host runner moves onto the new version itself between ticks, every checkout on the list with it (below).

##### Who runs it

The operator, in a checkout of the repo or naming one. It returns once that checkout's fleet instance has ended its first tick; the host runner ticks on, in the background, until it is stopped.

##### What it reads and writes

The checkout list: checkouts.json in the cache directory, kept on this host and never pushed. A checkout goes on it once its fleet instance's first tick ended, with the `--instance`, `--host` and `--worker-no-proxy` its `run` named; one refused before its first tick is not put there, and one there already stays there, broken (below). A `run` of a checkout on the list whose fleet instance does not run starts it with those, but for each that `run` names itself.

The checkout's concurrency, with its entry: how many claims its fleet instance holds at work at once on this host. `--concurrency 6` says it — a whole number, at least 1 — and `--concurrency default` changes it back to the default, 3; a `run` that names none leaves it as it is. Until the checkout says one, its fleet instance holds 3. It is said here and nowhere else: the repo config's `concurrency` is read no more, and `afkconvoy doctor` reports it as `info`, with the key to delete, first giving the `run` that keeps the config's number only where the checkout says none and the numbers differ. Unlike the `--instance`, `--host` and `--worker-no-proxy` it named, which hold from the start of its fleet instance, it is read at each tick, as the host settings are: a change holds at the next tick, and the fleet instance is never started again for it. Lowered below the claims held, it ends no worker: those claims are worked to the end — the tick's line counts those past it, as `holding 2/2 · 1 past the bound` — and no new one is taken until fewer are held. A checkout the list does not hold yet goes by it from its first tick, which puts it on the list with it. A host runner started again keeps it; `plan`, `doctor` and `checkouts` say the one in force and who says it.

The checkout's tracker, with its entry, read at each tick as its concurrency is: the repo its fleet reads and writes its issues in — the issues, their labels, comments, blockers, escalations and closing — while PRs, branches, the gate and their landing turns stay the checkout's own repo's (`docs/adr/0027`). `--tracker me/issues` says it, and `--tracker default`, or the checkout's own repo, says none; a `run` that names none leaves it as it is. Until the checkout says one, its tracker is its own repo. A tracker another repo than the checkout's holds the issues of many repos: the fleet works the open issues there that carry its repo's repo label, `repo:<owner>/<repo>`, and the ready label — in a bound repo, a flow label; every issue it or a worker opens there carries the repo label, and `intake` and `lock` give it to one that lacks it; and a PR or a landing commit names its issue `me/issues#7`, never `#7`, which is the checkout's own repo's. `run` makes the repo label, and the ready, escalate and lock labels of the repo config, in the tracker where it lacks them. It refuses to change the tracker while the checkout's fleet holds a claim on an issue of the tracker it had, or a legacy line still carries a PR of one, naming them, and changes nothing: run it again once they are done. The issues of the tracker it had stay there. A tracker GitHub says is public is refused, and nothing is made in it or changed: whoever can comment on an issue there writes what the fleet reads as its state and what a worker reads as its task. So is the checkout's own repo, where it is public and the checkout says no tracker, or `default`: every start of its fleet is refused until it says a private one, `--tracker <owner>/<private repo>`. A `run` that starts the host runner — where none runs, or where it moves one of an older release (below) — says the tracker of a checkout on the list with its entry before it starts it, as that host runner starts every checkout on the list, as its entry has it, before it is handed this one: it asks GitHub and makes the labels before an older host runner is stopped, which changes nothing where it refuses, and keeps the tracker once that host runner has let the host go. So its checkout's fleet instance starts under the tracker this `run` names, never under the one its entry had, and a checkout of a public repo is taken at the first `run --tracker <owner>/<private repo>`, whichever host runner was there. `plan`, `doctor`, `checkouts` and the panel say the tracker.

The host settings, in the same file: what this host says for every fleet instance on it — whether it may be put to sleep (`--no-host-sleep`, `--host-sleep`) and in which hours of its local time (`--host-sleep-hours`), the limits past which a worker is hot (`--hot-cores`, `--hot-memory`, `--hot-written`), the shares admission holds back at (`--admit-load`, `--admit-memory`, `--admit-disk`, `--admit-inspect-after`), the panel's port (`--panel`), the operator's directory a watch starts in and how often the host runner looks (`--watch-dir`, `--watch-every`; WATCH, below), and the command that prints the TypeSafe key Jev's worker-health judgments are asked with (`--jev-key-command`). A `run` that names one — by its flag, or by the variable of its environment that stands for it, the flag winning: AFKCONVOY_NO_HOST_SLEEP=true, AFKCONVOY_HOST_SLEEP_HOURS, AFKCONVOY_HOT_CORES, AFKCONVOY_HOT_MEMORY, AFKCONVOY_HOT_WRITTEN, AFKCONVOY_ADMIT_LOAD, AFKCONVOY_ADMIT_MEMORY, AFKCONVOY_ADMIT_DISK, AFKCONVOY_ADMIT_INSPECT_AFTER, AFKCONVOY_WATCH_DIR, AFKCONVOY_WATCH_EVERY, AFKCONVOY_JEV_KEY_COMMAND — changes it for the host before it hands its checkout over. Every fleet instance on the host reads them as it goes — admission at each tick, the hot limits at each sample, host sleep at each check, the watch's before each look, the key command at each worker-health judgment — so a change holds for all of them at once, and none is started again for it; the host runner reads the panel's port as it starts. A `run` that names none changes none, and nothing else changes them: `tick`, `plan` and `doctor` read them as they are, and a host runner started again keeps them. `--host-sleep` changes `--no-host-sleep` back, and `default` changes any other back to its default (`--hot-cores default`, `--host-sleep-hours default`). `afkconvoy doctor` says those in force, as `host.settings`.

The host runner: one process of the host, holding a fleet instance for each checkout on the list, each ticking as a fleet instance always has. `run` asks it on its socket in the cache directory (host-runner.sock) — the one socket of the host: `stop`, `wake`, `panel --open`, `exclusive` and `doctor` ask it there too, each naming its checkout, and no fleet instance or repo has one of its own; one nobody listens on, which a host runner killed with no goodbye left, is removed by whoever finds it — and starts it where none answers: in a process group of its own, so the terminal that ran `run` can close, in /, with a fresh login shell's environment — the names your login shell (`$SHELL -lic`) exports, and none of those of the shell that ran `run`. A variable exported only in that shell, or one a session set for itself (Claude Code's, orca's), reaches neither the host runner nor any worker it starts: put it in your login shell's rc files. It keeps the cache directory and the config directory of the `run` that started it. Started again, it starts every checkout on the list, each with what its `run` named, under the host settings the file keeps; a checkout whose fleet instance cannot start then is broken (below), and stays on the list.

Before anything else, `run` asks the host runner for its version. One of an older release than this `run`'s — after `brew upgrade afkconvoy` — is stopped as SIGTERM stops it: each fleet instance finishes the step it is in, and the checkout list is kept. Once it has let the host go, `run` starts a host runner of its own version, which starts every checkout on the same list, and then adds its own — saying its checkout's tracker with its entry there first, where it names one (above). What the old one held for every fleet instance goes with it: the next one's fleet instances count as idle for host sleep from their first tick, a watch goes on in its terminal with its original time limit, and an `exclusive` command waiting in the old one's queue waits in the next one's, from when it first asked (`afkconvoy exclusive --help`). One of a newer release refuses this `run`, which changes nothing. A build past a release (`afkconvoy --version` says `0.6.0+11.g9f58035`) is of that release, and one of the same release as the host runner's is handed the checkout as ever.

The host runner moves onto a newer release by itself, with nothing run by hand. It watches the file it was started from — the path the `run` that started it was run as, such as the link Homebrew keeps, /opt/homebrew/bin/afkconvoy — and within 1s of a change there, as `brew upgrade afkconvoy` makes, asks it `--version`. Once a newer release answers, it pauses new ticks and new exclusive commands, lets active ticks and the running exclusive command finish, and moves between ticks. A command waiting in the exclusive queue holds nothing back: it rejoins the new runner with when it first asked. Claims stamped with this host, workers in their terminals, PRs waiting to land, a cut and a watch all carry over; no worker is stopped. It waits at most 600s for that moment. If it still cannot move, it lets ticks and the queue run again on the old release, and `afkconvoy doctor` gives a finding with what held it, as `host.installed.held_back`; it keeps trying the move automatically, while the finding stays visible. `host.installed.since` is when that file answered, in epoch seconds; `wait_expired` says that this wait expired. Then each fleet instance stops between two ticks, keeping its `stop` line, and the host runner starts the newer afkconvoy's in its place, with the same checkout list and host settings, and lets the host go to it. That one starts every checkout on the list, each where its fleet instance left off; `checkouts` and the next `run` answer its pid and version. It never moves onto an older release, nor onto a build of its own release. One that does not start, or does not answer within 35s, leaves the old host runner holding the host and starting every checkout on the list again; `afkconvoy doctor` then gives a finding naming it, as it does for one there that does not say its version, and the host runner tries that file again only once it changes. The move, with both releases and what carried over, is a line of the host runner's log and of each checkout's tick log — `moved`, or `not_moved` with why it did not start — which `doctor` lists among its events.

The host runner's log: host-runner.log in the cache directory, moved aside to host-runner.log.1 once past a MiB. One line, stamped in UTC, as it starts and as it stops, as it replaces a host runner of an older release (`host runner upgraded: from afkconvoy 0.5.13 (pid 4100) to afkconvoy 0.6.0 (pid 4242)`), as it finds another release installed where it was started from, as nothing holds the move back any more, as it moves onto it (`host runner moved: from afkconvoy 0.6.0 (pid 4242) to afkconvoy 0.6.1 (pid 4300), installed at /opt/homebrew/bin/afkconvoy`) or that one does not start (`host runner not moved: …`, with what it said as it ended), as each fleet instance starts and ends, as one breaks and is back, as a checkout is added, refused or removed, as anything in it panics (`panicked at <file>:<line>: <what it said>`), where it serves the panel, as it starts (`panel: http://127.0.0.1:7070/`), and each line a fleet instance says outside its tick log, after its checkout: its warnings and the `start:` lines after its first:

```
fleet instance broken: /Users/me/Developments/hkj: it panicked: <what it said> · since 2026-10-24 09:12:00 UTC · started again at 2026-10-24 09:13:00 UTC, in 60s
fleet instance back: /Users/me/Developments/hkj: me-h1-5e6f7a8b, broken since 2026-10-24 09:12:00 UTC, for 75s
```

Two kinds of checkout are refused, with an error: one whose fleet instance is refused before its first tick — it fails the startup probe, say — which is not put on the list, and stays on it, broken (below), where it was on it already, whichever start was refused — the host runner's, as it starts or moves, or this `run`'s; and a second checkout of a repo already on the list, a clone or a worktree of it: a host runs one fleet instance per repo, and the error names the checkout to run it from.

A fleet instance is broken when its loop panics or ends in an error, or when a start of it ends before its first tick while its checkout is on the list — the host runner's, from the list or after it broke, or a `run`'s: its startup probe no longer passes, say. It harms no other: the host runner and every other fleet instance go on, and its checkout stays on the list. The host runner starts it again after a backoff: 1 minute after it first broke, twice the wait before at each break in a row — one within 30 minutes of the start before it — and 30 minutes at the most. A `run` of its checkout starts it at once, with what that `run` names laid over what the list kept; a start of it that ends before its first tick is then refused to that `run`, which is told so, and it stays on the list, broken. Only `stop` takes a checkout off the list. It is back once a start of it again has ended its first tick. Broken — with why, since when, and when it is started again — and back are lines of the host runner's log and of its tick log, and `afkconvoy doctor` in its checkout says it is broken, why, and when it is started again. A tick that fails is no break: it is a line of its own, and the loop goes on.

Then everything a fleet instance does. It makes the startup probe — at every start, whatever probe passed before — takes every claim stamped with this host — on an issue, on a patrol's run, on the proposal of a precedent — removes the heartbeats that are dead and hold nothing (those of the instances it took from, this host's past the lease, anyone's older than a day) — then ticks: each tick rebuilds the working set from GitHub and the remote and makes every transition it calls for — claims and heartbeats on the remote, workers in orca worktrees, comments, labels and blocked-by edges on issues, status boards, the landing turn's worker. Between ticks it sleeps; a worker's `wake` ends the sleep, and a tick that left the next one a worker to start is followed with no sleep. Before each tick it asks GitHub again whether its tracker is public, once the check that found it private is an hour old — or at once, of a tracker said anew. Public, it ends before the tick, as its startup probe would refuse it, and is broken: it keeps no host awake and holds no move onto a newer release back, and each start of it again is refused until the tracker is private again or another is said (`--tracker`), which `afkconvoy doctor` names with that line.

Once every fleet on this host has been idle 10 minutes it puts the host to sleep (`pmset sleepnow`) — a host sleep — within the host's sleep hours, unless the host settings keep it awake: `--no-host-sleep`, for every fleet on it, until a `run` says `--host-sleep`. The sleep hours are 00:00-06:00 of the host's local time, unless its host settings say others: `--host-sleep-hours 22:00-06:00`, until a `run` says `--host-sleep-hours default`, which changes them back. The fleet never wakes the host: one put to sleep within its sleep hours sleeps on past their end, until something else wakes it. Idle is holding no claim — on an issue, a patrol's run, a proposal, a cut — nothing on the base branch, and an empty frontier; an escalated issue and a patrol not yet due leave a fleet idle. A cut is started by a fleet that goes idle, and keeps it from idle, and the host awake, while it runs. Every fleet on this host is a fleet instance of its one host runner, which holds how each stands, as each says it as every tick of its ends: whether it keeps the host awake, since when it has been idle or not, and when it last worked. No fleet instance asks another.

ADMISSION. A tick starts no new worker while its host is busy: its 1-minute load average past 200% of its cores, less than 10% of its memory free (what the kernel counts as available: `sysctl kern.memorystatus_level`, or MemAvailable in /proc/meminfo), or less than 1% of the disk under the checkout free (`df`). The issue stays on the frontier for the next tick, and so do a stale claim, a due patrol and a due proposal. Workers already running are left alone, and so is the worker a declared verdict starts. The host says its own shares, each a whole percent, in its host settings: `--admit-load` (of its cores), `--admit-memory` and `--admit-disk` (free) — `--admit-load 400` lets the load reach four times the cores, and `--admit-disk 0` never holds for disk. A value that is no whole percent is refused, and `default` changes a share back. What cannot be read holds nothing back. `plan` and `doctor` say the thresholds in force and what the host reads.

When admission holds back for one reason — load, memory or disk — at every tick for ten minutes (`--admit-inspect-after` sets the host's span), doctor names a finding that starts the host's watch at its next look. Reasons that change start none. Memory pressure (macOS's level at least 2) held for the same span is its own finding, even while admission admits, and never makes a worker hot. Each episode ends after five minutes of recovery. The watch receives the condition, how long it held, admission's reading and shares, and host evidence: for disk, each fleet's worktrees and caches and the largest directories outside them; for load or memory, worker process trees and the hottest processes outside them. It checks admission or pressure itself after acting. Resource readings continue during a watch; new triggers wait for the next look, and an episode already watched starts nothing again, including across a host runner move.

WATCH. Every host watches itself. Where its host settings name an operator's directory — `--watch-dir ~/Developments/control`, known to orca — the watch runs there under that directory's own rules, with none of the stock instruction added. Otherwise the stock watch runs in the fleet's own directory, `stock-watch/` under the cache directory (`afkconvoy help cache` says where it is), made, kept and registered with orca when it starts. Its short instruction carried in the binary says: find what holds the fleets' work back, fix it with the watch's authority, check that the work goes on and say what it did. Every watch leaves spending money or needing an account, a credential or a person's hands; what cannot be undone; taking a secret or private data off the host; and changing what a product is for or who it is for with a human, acts on none and lists each in its printed record, which `doctor` lists as `did`. Unplaced host kit models are low priority: a watch started for other work takes them too, and they alone start a watch at most once a day, across runner restarts. The watch researches them with its web tools and places them through `afkconvoy kit --research <file>` (`afkconvoy kit --help` gives the checked file format). Its host runner takes a look every 300 seconds (`--watch-every`): `afkconvoy doctor --all --since <until of its last look>`, the fleet's own code, which runs no model, keeping `until` itself. A look that holds something an operator would act on — an issue waiting on a human, a finding that holds something up, a fleet instance not alive or broken, a failed tick or step, a worker whose health observation is past its time — starts one watch, once per episode of each such thing: an episode lasts while each look still holds it. A watch is an agent session in the watch directory, given its brief as a file in the cache directory — what the look answered, why it started, and what each earlier watch on the same items did — with authority over the fleets of this host and an hour, its continuations together. It runs on the harness this host last started a worker on that took its brief, then the host kit's order, never one paused or with a fault on record, started trusted and in its harness's non-interactive mode, so that nothing it runs waits on a prompt; its terminal, titled "afkconvoy watch", exits with the harness, beside whatever else is open in that directory, which it never closes. What it prints is kept as what it did. A watch whose harness gives out — its usage limit, or an exit that failed — is ended and continued on the next harness that can start it, with the same look and what it printed so far, one session at a time; the fault is recorded (`host_kit.worker_health`), and that harness is skipped until its hourly probe answers. While a watch runs no look is taken: what one would find is in the first look after the watch ends. A host runner started again — after moving onto a newer release, say — keeps the watch it finds running. Its start, its end and each thing it did are lines of every tick log on the checkout list and of the host runner's log; `doctor` says the watch running and the last one, as `host.watch`, and a critical finding where no harness could start or continue it. `--watch-dir default` returns to the stock watch; a running watch and its continuations keep their starting directory and rules. `doctor.host.watch.directory` says the directory the next watch runs in, and `stock` whether it is the stock one, even before a watch starts; each running or last watch says its own directory and `stock` too.

The watch operates for every repo on the checkout list (`afkconvoy checkouts`), bound or unbound. It may trust a worktree for a harness, restart, nudge, continue or switch a worker and change host settings. Once the cause of a fleet fault is gone it hands the escalated issue back with its current `doctor.waiting_on_human.answer` line, naming that repo's tracker, wakes the checkout after a `gh` change and checks that the next tick dispatches or continues it and its worker takes its brief. The watch answers escalations with `rule`, handing back, `send`, closing or changing blocked-by, using the same commands as a human and starting rework counts over. Both watch directories leave only the four human kinds above, listing each question and answer line in the watch's record; `doctor` lists what it did.

A lasting fix may be code in any listed repo, even one whose fleet cannot start workers. The watch makes it in a linked worktree of its own from that repo's configured base branch, named `afkconvoy-watch` or `afkconvoy-watch-<digits>`, on its own branch; never in another worker's or watch's checkout. It commits and pushes, opens the PR against that repo's base branch on no issue, then takes a turn with `afkconvoy land --watch` to merge, gate, record green and land. This reuses a watch's landing path and attribution, with no intake or flow label, and respects fleet locks. It records the repo and PR.

When the fix must reach an installed tool, the watch waits for landing and has that repo's fleet cut a version through its declared cut steps (`afkconvoy cut --help`): it wakes the checkout, reads `plan.cut` and fixes what holds back the next idle tick. A mechanically failed cut is continued with its report's `cut --from <step>` line once its cause is fixed. It checks publication and installation; for afkconvoy, it lets the host runner move onto the version itself, reading `doctor`'s `host.installed` and `checkouts`'s host runner version, never killing or restarting it. Then it repeats the check that showed the fault and checks that the work goes on. Its transcript records each fix, PR, cut, version and evidence, the four human kinds left alone and anything still pending; landing or installing alone proves no recovery. All fits within the watch's one hour: anything unfinished is recorded as pending.

A fleet instance idle 10 minutes checks then, tick due or not, whatever the hour, and again 10 minutes after a check that kept the host awake — or, where that is outside the sleep hours, as they start. It puts the host to sleep only when all hold:

- the host's local time (`localtime_r`: TZ, else /etc/localtime) is within its sleep hours, the start included and the end not: with 00:00-06:00, 05:59 is and 06:00 is not;
- it worked — held a claim, or had something on the base branch — since the host last woke (`sysctl kern.waketime`): a host woken, by hand or otherwise, stays awake until a fleet on it works again;
- every fleet instance on the host, as the host runner holds how it stands, keeps the host awake none, and each has been idle 10 minutes;
- nobody touched the keyboard or mouse for ten minutes (HIDIdleTime, from `ioreg`);
- every fleet instance, itself included, ticks once more — each other one woken to — and each still finds nothing: idle, as before.

One check is made on the host at a time: while one waits for the others' ticks, no other fleet instance checks. It waits for a tick each began after it was woken, however long that takes, and no longer for one that ended meanwhile. A check whose own fleet instance is woken while it waits — something changed for its fleet — or told to stop ends there, with the host awake; it is checked again later.

It samples each worker every ten seconds. A hot worker becomes a doctor finding and starts the host's watch once per episode. Its look carries the worker, issue, worktree, terminal, condition, duration and the evidence taken down as it turned hot: process tree, five-second sample, resident memory, disk writes and largest directories. The watch takes no slot of concurrency. There is one watch per host, with one hour shared by its continuations.

Each fleet instance also keeps a log on this host, its tick log, in a file under the cache directory (runs/; `afkconvoy help cache` says where it is and what moves it): one line when it starts, one as each tick starts — with why, and the command whose wake started it — and one as it ends — what `tick` answers for it — and one of each event that reached it: a wake heard during a tick, a check for host sleep, the host waking, being told to stop. Every command that changes fleet state writes a line of its own to the same file as it acts (its `--help` says so under "What it logs", and [`afkconvoy help tick-log`](help:tick-log) says what the line holds). It keeps every line of the last 24 hours, and never fewer than 200 lines nor more than 5000. A line is written whole as it happens, so killing the host runner loses none, and none a command appends while the fleet instance cuts the file back is lost. Nothing reads the log to decide anything; `afkconvoy doctor` reads it to say what the last ticks did, which steps failed, and the wakes, starts, stops and host sleeps of late.

##### What it answers

Before a first start: a checkout off the checkout list must name `--tracker <owner>/<repo>` or `--tracker default` (its own repo, which must be private). A host with no saved host settings must name `--host-sleep`, `--no-host-sleep` or `--host-sleep-hours`. Missing answers refuse with a non-zero exit and write nothing: {"error", "asks", "see"}. Each `asks` item has `setting`, `question`, `default`, `recommend`, and `options`, each with `option` and `line`; `see` prints [`afkconvoy help first-start`](help:first-start). Settle these questions with the user before running the chosen lines. Existing checkouts and saved host settings run as before.

Once its checkout's fleet instance has ended its first tick, with exit 0:

```json
{"checkout": "/Users/me/Developments/hkj", "repo": "github.com/me/hkj", "added": true,
 "instance": "me-h1-1a2b3c4d",
 "host_runner": {"pid": 4242, "version": "0.6.0", "log": "<cache>/host-runner.log",
                 "panel": "http://127.0.0.1:7070/", "started": true, "replaced": null},
 "tick_log": "<cache>/runs/hkj-0123456789abcdef.jsonl",
 "first_tick": "tick 1: dispatched #12, #15 · holding 2/6 · frontier 4 · next in 30s",
 "concurrency": {"from": {"in_force": 3, "said_by": "default"},
                 "to": {"in_force": 6, "said_by": "checkout"}},
 "tracker": {"from": null, "to": "me/issues"},
 "settings": {"hot_cores": {"from": null, "to": 4.0}},
 "warnings": []}
```

- `repo`: the repo the checkout is of, as its remote `origin` names it.
- `added`: false when the checkout was on the list already. Where its fleet instance runs, the flags of this `run` that are its fleet instance's own change nothing, and the answer is that instance, with its own first tick.
- `host_runner`: the one that answered — its pid, its version, its log and where it serves the panel, null where it serves none — and whether this `run` started it. `replaced`: the host runner of an older release this `run` stopped to start it, as {"pid": 4100, "version": "0.5.13"}; null where it stopped none.
- `tick_log` and `first_tick`: the fleet instance's tick log, and the line that ended its first tick. `<cache>` stands for the cache directory, whole in the answer.
- `concurrency`: what this `run` changed of its checkout's concurrency, as {from, to}, each the one in force before and after, as `plan` says it: {in_force, said_by} — said_by `checkout` or `default`. null where it named none, or named the one in force.
- `tracker`: what this `run` changed of its checkout's tracker, as {from, to}, each the repo named, `<owner>/<repo>`, or null for the checkout's own. null where it named none, or named the one it has. A `run` that kept it with its checkout's entry before it started the host runner says it in an error the host runner answered too: the tracker stays said.
- `settings`: what this `run` changed of the host settings, each by its key — its flag's name, as `hot_cores` for `--hot-cores` — as {from, to}, in its flag's units; null is the default. {} where it named none, or named each as it was.
- `warnings`: what its fleet instance warned of until its first tick ended — the startup probe's warnings among them — also on stderr; empty where this `run` waited on no start.

Each fleet instance's lines — `run` prints none of them. Its tick log holds them, and `afkconvoy doctor` reads them back, but for the `start:` lines after the first — the terms of host sleep, and the claims its start took — which are lines of the host runner's log, after the checkout (`/Users/me/Developments/hkj: start: took #4, #7 stamped with this host`):

```
start: run as tester-h1-1a2b3c4d on h1, its workers started with `claude`
start: puts this host to sleep within its sleep hours, 00:00-06:00, once every fleet on it has been idle 10 minutes (`--host-sleep-hours` says others, `--no-host-sleep` keeps it awake)
start: took #4, #7 stamped with this host        only when a start took or lost claims
start: took #4, the run of the patrol sweep stamped with this host
start: took #4 stamped with this host · swept 1 dead heartbeat(s) that held nothing
stop: holding no claim, it took its heartbeat with it
stop: it left its heartbeat with the claims it holds: the next start on this host takes them
tick 1: started (start)
tick 1: dispatched #12, #15 · holding 2/3 · frontier 4 · next in 30s
tick 2: started (timer)
woken by park #46 during tick 2: tick 3 follows
tick 2: nothing to do · holding 2/3 · frontier 4 · next in 60s
tick 3: advanced #12 → review · dispatched #12 · holding 2/3 · frontier 0 · next in 90s
tick 4: advanced #12 → land · holding 1/3 · frontier 0 · next now
tick 5: dispatched #12 · holding 2/3 · frontier 0 · next in 90s
tick 6: escalated #15 (workup: consult let it through) · holding 1/3 · frontier 0 · next now
tick 7: dispatched #71 · skipped #68 (blocked by #71) · holding 2/3 · frontier 0 · next in 90s
```

The second `start:` line is there unless the host settings keep the host awake as it starts. Every tick has a line as it starts, before it does anything, naming why: `timer` (its sleep ran out), `woken` (a wake ended the sleep, or was heard during the tick before: `woken by` the command that sent it, and what that acted on, where it named them), `start` (the fleet instance's first) or `follow-up` (the tick before left a worker to start, or could not reach GitHub, so it runs with no sleep). A wake heard during a tick is a line as it is heard — the first of each tick — and the next tick starts as that one ends: ticks never overlap. A check for host sleep is a line, and so is the host waking from a sleep, as the fleet instance notices it — a rest that took a minute past its length — and being told to stop:

```
tick 4: started (woken by verdict #121)
tick 4: started (woken)                          a wake that named nothing
tick 5: started (follow-up)
host sleep: every fleet on this host has been idle long enough, and ticked once more: put the host to sleep
host sleep: kept awake: the keyboard or mouse was used 40s ago
host sleep: kept awake: the host could not be put to sleep: <why>
host woke: after 3600s asleep
```

The host runner keeps two lines of its own in a fleet instance's tick log: as it breaks, and as it is back.

```
broken: it panicked: <what it said> · since 2026-10-24 09:12:00 UTC · started again at 2026-10-24 09:13:00 UTC, in 60s
back: broken since 2026-10-24 09:12:00 UTC, for 75s
```

A tick's line names what it did — lost, escalated, released, left, settled, ended, advanced, unlocked, reclaimed, dispatched, skipped (a frontier issue found blocked just before its claim, with what blocks it), nudged, waiting on its own background work (with since when: `#7 (since 2026-10-20 23:03 UTC, 12m ago)`), continued, restarted — then, when admission held back a worker it would have started, which threshold did (`admission holds back new workers: the load 31.20 is past 28.00, 200% of its 14 cores`), then the claims held out of the concurrency, and the frontier left. The claims a fleet lock has it leave alone take no slot and are counted apart (`holding 1/3 · 2 left alone`), and so are those whose worker declared a verdict not acted on yet (`holding 3/3 · 1 declared`), as are those past the bound — a start took them, or the checkout's concurrency was lowered under them (`holding 3/3 · 1 past the bound`). A step that failed is in the line as `FAILED <step> #<issue>: <why>`, and a tick that could not start as `tick N: FAILED: <why>`; the loop goes on either way. One cause that stopped several steps is said once: `FAILED 7 steps: <why>`.

`advanced #12 → review`: the tick read a verdict that left #12 at `review`. Where a role performs that stage the same tick starts its worker, and says so: `dispatched #12`. An issue advanced to no stage — its workflow ended, or it was parked — is named alone.

`escalated #15 (workup: consult let it through)`: the tick handed #15 to a human, whichever step did, with why in a few words — the stage first, where it was at one. It is named as nothing else. The comment on the issue says why in full and ends with the line that answers it; `afkconvoy doctor` lists it under `waiting_on_human`.

Between ticks a fleet instance sleeps 90 seconds while it has work, or 25 minutes once 3 ticks in a row were empty. Commands that change fleet state wake it sooner, as does `afkconvoy wake`. A fleet on this host that closes an issue or sees it closed wakes every other fleet on the same tracker whose open issues it blocked, across repos. The wake names the closed issue and the fleet instance that saw it, in the woken fleet's tick log. Even with another blocker still open the fleet is woken; that next tick reads GitHub and takes up only what is unblocked. A change made on GitHub, or by another host's fleet, is read at the next tick: no webhook reaches the host. Where the tick acts on such a change, its line says what changed since the tick before, and who changed it where that is known:

```
tick 8: lost #46 to instance beta-1a2b3c4d on host h2 (takeover) · holding 1/3 · frontier 0 · next in 90s
tick 9: dispatched #45 (labelled ready-for-agent since tick 8) · holding 2/3 · frontier 0 · next in 90s
tick 9: released #231 (the issue was deleted) · holding 1/3 · frontier 0 · next in 90s
tick 9: left #97 (closed by @alice) · holding 1/3 · frontier 0 · next now
tick 9: skipped #320 (blocked by #379, added since tick 8) · holding 1/3 · frontier 0 · next in 90s
```

`lost #46`: a claim this instance held is another's now — taken by a takeover, or `(stale: past the lease)`, as a stale claim, this instance's heartbeat being past the lease. `released #231`: its issue was deleted, or `(the issue is gone from this repo)`, transferred. `left #97`: a claim with no PR whose issue was closed, by whoever GitHub says closed it (`closed on GitHub` where it says no one), is settled — nothing of the fleet's landed. `labelled …` and `added since …` say what the tick before saw otherwise. A change the tick does nothing about is in no line; nor is one made before the fleet instance's first tick, which has no tick before it, nor anything of the kind in what `afkconvoy tick` answers.

`next now` in place of `next in <n>s`: the tick settled an issue, or advanced one without starting what follows, and left a slot free, so what follows — a consult, the landing of a PR, an issue the landing unblocked — is the next tick's to start, and that tick starts with no sleep.

So does the tick after one that failed on a read GitHub could not be reached for (`GitHub could not be reached: …`): nothing says the next read fails too. At most 4 ticks run back to back; then it sleeps, whatever the last one left.

The host runner serves the panel from its start until it ends, on the panel's port of the host settings — 7070 where they say none, or any free port where that one is taken: every fleet of the host as one web page — the host first, then what waits for a human across every repo, then each repo with its workflows as lines of their stages and its landing turns — brought up to date in the browser after every tick of any fleet instance, by itself. `afkconvoy panel --help` says what the page shows, and `afkconvoy panel --open` where it is served. Its address is a line of the host runner's log:

```
panel: http://127.0.0.1:7070/
```

`--panel <port>` sets that port, a host setting, which the host runner reads as it starts: one that runs already serves the panel where it does, and the next one — after `afkconvoy stop --all`, or an upgrade — on the port set.

Errors, before the first tick, as {"error": …} with a non-zero exit: the host is not macOS and its host settings do not keep it awake (`--no-host-sleep`), or this `run` says `--host-sleep` there; the host settings cannot be read or written; a command the fleet needs is missing or logged out, or orca is not running or does not know this checkout (the error names each, with the line to run); the repo fails the startup probe; its tracker — the one `--tracker` names, or the one the checkout says — is public (the error names it, with the line that says a private one); the config cannot be read; the host kit cannot be read; the worker launch command of a harness the fleet could be asked for resolves to nothing, or does not take the flags the fleet adds for its role or worktree trust; another checkout of the repo is on the checkout list; the checkout has no remote `origin`; the login shell did not answer within 20 seconds; the host runner is of a newer release than this `run` (the error names both versions, and nothing was changed); the host runner did not say its version within 10 seconds; the host runner of an older release, told to stop, still held the host after 30 seconds; no host runner answered within 35 seconds; the host runner ended before it answered, or is stopping; the checkout's fleet instance is stopping, told by `afkconvoy stop`; no first tick within 30 minutes; the checkout list cannot be written. Each error a host runner gave says which, as `host_runner`.

##### What trips you up

- Stop the host runner with `afkconvoy stop --all`, or SIGTERM to its pid, `host_runner.pid` in any `run`'s answer: each fleet instance finishes the step it is in, makes none of the steps left in its tick, and ends — within a second when it sleeps — and the host runner exits once every one has, keeping the checkout list: the next `run` starts every checkout on it. No claim is released on the way out and no worker is stopped: the workers work on, and the next start on this host takes the claims back. Holding no claim, a fleet instance removes its heartbeat from the remote; holding one, it leaves it, and that next start removes it. A second signal ends the host runner at once, as SIGKILL does, with no goodbye: what that leaves, a later start on this host removes once it is past the lease. A patrol's run and a proposal it takes back are ended by its first tick once their worker is gone or has stopped, as any run of its own.
- Ctrl-C while `run` waits ends that `run` alone: the host runner is in a process group of its own, and goes on with the checkout.
- Of a `run` whose checkout's fleet instance runs already, the flags that are that instance's own — `--instance`, `--host`, `--worker-no-proxy` — change nothing: `afkconvoy stop` it, and run again with those you want. `afkconvoy stop --help` says how to stop one checkout and how to stop them all. The host settings it names change all the same, for that instance and every other on the host, and so does its checkout's `--concurrency`, for that instance alone, from its next tick.
- A checkout's concurrency is that checkout's, on this host: another host works the repo at its own, and a checkout that says none holds 3. How many workers a repo gets at once is what the host can carry — its cores, its memory, its logins — and no fact of the repo, so the repo config says none: a `concurrency` it still names is read no more. Raising it for an afternoon, or lowering it while the host is needed for something else, is one `run`, and no commit.
- Without `--instance` each start mints a new instance id, named for this host: the answer says it as `instance`, and `afkconvoy doctor` as `fleet.instance`, for `plan --instance` and the commands that make one transition by hand.
- A host setting is the host's, not a `run`'s or a repo's: `--hot-cores 4` named in one checkout holds for every fleet instance on the host until a `run` names it again, and `--hot-cores default` changes it back. The variables that stand for the flags are read from the environment of a `run` and of nothing else — not of the host runner, nor of `tick`, `plan` or `doctor` — so one exported in your shell's rc files is named again by every `run` started from that shell.
- The panel is served to this host only, and shows a tick, not this second: between two ticks it changes nothing but its countdown. It costs GitHub no read of its own.
- Every worker launch command comes from the host kit: run `afkconvoy kit` to write it again. It is $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/afkconvoy/kit.json, or $HOME/.config/afkconvoy/kit.json, kept on this host and never pushed. `--worker-command` is gone. On a host with no host kit, `run` writes one as `afkconvoy kit` does, at a terminal or not, asking nothing: it says on stderr where the file is, what it holds and what was left out, and goes on to its first tick. At each worker launch the latest kit is read; a known harness with no entry or command is discovered in the login shell and its checked stock command merged into the kit without model probes. Explicit commands are respected, including errors. Harness selection follows host kit order within role eligibility.
- The fleet starts every worker launch command under `nice`, with a `TMPDIR` of the worktree's own, adding its harness's model flag where the worker runs a model — and, in a bound repo, what puts the worker in its role, under the guard: [`afkconvoy help worker-launch`](help:worker-launch) says, harness by harness, the line each worker is started with, what each part is for and what loads from where.
- In a bound repo, before any worker is started, the command of every harness the fleet could be asked for is checked: the host kit's first, each harness of each role's range (`afkconvoy help roster`). One that cannot be started refuses the start, named with its harness and the range that calls for it, and no worker at all is started: no harness is ever started in another's place. So does a role whose range on this host is empty: the refusal names the role, what the roster allows it, what the host kit holds and what the range leaves out. A range leaves out each harness the role holds no limits for while it holds limits for another, so no worker runs a harness it holds no limits for; `plan` and `check` name each harness left out.

##### Worker proxy bypass

A start on this host reaches some hosts past the proxy with `--worker-no-proxy [HARNESS=]HOSTS`, never a key of the repo's config: [`afkconvoy help worker-proxy`](help:worker-proxy) says what each worker is given.

##### Which checkout it is about

Name it after the command, as `[CHECKOUT]`: a checkout of the repo, or any directory in one, which names that checkout. Naming none, it is about the checkout it is run in. A worker's worktree is refused as its checkout: only a worker's own commands, and those that only read, are run there.

##### Usage

```
afkconvoy run [OPTIONS] [CHECKOUT]
```

##### Arguments

- `[CHECKOUT]`: The checkout it is about, or a directory in it [default: the one it is run in]
- `--instance <INSTANCE>`: The fleet instance to run as [default: a new one, named for this host]
- `--host <HOST>`
- `--concurrency <CLAIMS>`: How many claims this checkout's fleet instance holds at work at once on this host, from its next tick: the checkout's own, kept with it on the checkout list and never pushed; `default` changes it back [default: 3]
- `--tracker <OWNER/REPO>`: The private repo this checkout's fleet reads and writes its issues in: required on its first `run`; kept on this host and never pushed. `default` says its own repo explicitly, which must be private; omitted on later runs, its saved choice holds
- `--worker-no-proxy <[HARNESS=]HOSTS>`: Hosts reached directly, comma-separated, for the default harness or HARNESS; repeat for each harness. DSH defaults to api.deepseek.com. An empty list disables the stock addition. Extends no_proxy and NO_PROXY
- `--panel <PORT>`: The port the host runner serves the panel on, from its next start: a host setting; `default` changes it back [default: 7070, or any free port where it is taken]
- `--watch-dir <DIR>`: The operator's directory this host starts a watch in, when a look finds something to act on: a host setting; `default` uses the stock watch in afkconvoy's own directory [default: stock watch]
  - Environment: `AFKCONVOY_WATCH_DIR`
- `--watch-every <SECONDS>`: Seconds between this host's looks: a host setting; `default` changes it back [default: 300]
  - Environment: `AFKCONVOY_WATCH_EVERY`
- `--no-host-sleep`: Keep this host awake: no fleet on it puts it to sleep. A host setting, for every fleet on it until a `run` says `--host-sleep`, which changes it back
  - Environment: `AFKCONVOY_NO_HOST_SLEEP`
- `--host-sleep`: Let the fleets on this host put it to sleep once every one has been idle ten minutes, within its sleep hours, as they do by default: a host setting, for every fleet on it. Said, it holds over `--no-host-sleep` and its variable
- `--host-sleep-hours <HH:MM-HH:MM>`: The hours of this host's local time a fleet may put it to sleep in, from the first, included, to the second, not — past midnight where the second comes first (22:00-06:00); 00:00-24:00 is any hour: a host setting, for every fleet on it; `default` changes them back [default: 00:00-06:00]
  - Environment: `AFKCONVOY_HOST_SLEEP_HOURS`
- `--hot-cores <CORES>`: The cores a worker's processes may take before it turns hot, held two minutes: a host setting; `default` changes it back [default: half this host's cores, one at the least]
  - Environment: `AFKCONVOY_HOT_CORES`
- `--hot-memory <GIB>`: The GiB of memory a worker's processes may hold resident before it turns hot: a host setting; `default` changes it back [default: a quarter of this host's memory]
  - Environment: `AFKCONVOY_HOT_MEMORY`
- `--hot-written <GIB>`: The GiB a worker's processes may write to disk in ten minutes before it turns hot: a host setting; `default` changes it back [default: a tenth of the disk free here, one GiB at the least]
  - Environment: `AFKCONVOY_HOT_WRITTEN`
- `--admit-load <PERCENT>`: The load, a whole percent of this host's cores, past which no tick starts a new worker: a host setting; `default` changes it back [default: 200]
  - Environment: `AFKCONVOY_ADMIT_LOAD`
- `--admit-memory <PERCENT>`: The memory free, a whole percent of this host's, under which no tick starts a new worker: a host setting; `default` changes it back [default: 10]
  - Environment: `AFKCONVOY_ADMIT_MEMORY`
- `--admit-disk <PERCENT>`: The disk free, a whole percent of the checkout's, under which no tick starts a new worker — 0 never holds for disk: a host setting; `default` changes it back [default: 1]
  - Environment: `AFKCONVOY_ADMIT_DISK`
- `--admit-inspect-after <SECONDS>`: The seconds admission holds back for one reason before the condition starts a watch: a host setting; `default` changes it back [default: 600]
  - Environment: `AFKCONVOY_ADMIT_INSPECT_AFTER`
- `--exclusive-seconds <SECONDS>`: Seconds a running exclusive command may hold others up, counting only while another waits: a host setting; `default` changes it back [default: 1200]
  - Environment: `AFKCONVOY_EXCLUSIVE_SECONDS`
- `--jev-key-command <COMMAND>`: The shell command whose stdout is the TypeSafe key Jev is asked with when it judges a stopped worker's screen, such as one that reads the key from a keychain: a host setting, run afresh for each check. The key is sent only to TypeSafe, and is in no file, answer or log line; a command that fails or prints nothing is an error, and the worker waits for the operator as with none. `default` removes it [default: none]
  - Environment: `AFKCONVOY_JEV_KEY_COMMAND`
- `--gate-lanes <GATE_LANES>`: Worker lanes on this host, above zero, or `default` (1). A repo holds at most one turn at a time, regardless of this count
  - Environment: `AFKCONVOY_GATE_LANES`

#### `afkconvoy stop`

Take a checkout off this host's checkout list and stop its fleet instance, or with `--all` stop the host runner and keep the list

##### When to run it

To stop working one repo on this host and leave the others worked: `afkconvoy stop` in its checkout, or naming it. To stop every repo — to start every fleet instance again with flags of its own, say — `afkconvoy stop --all`: the next `run`, in any checkout, starts every checkout on the list again. An upgrade needs none: the host runner moves onto the new release by itself between ticks (`afkconvoy run --help`).

##### Who runs it

The operator, in a checkout on the list or naming one; with `--all`, anywhere on this host.

##### What it reads and writes

The checkout list: checkouts.json in the cache directory. `stop` takes the checkout off it; `--all` leaves it as it is.

The host runner, spoken to on its socket in the cache directory (host-runner.sock), naming the checkout. Its fleet instance of the checkout — every one, with `--all` — stops as SIGTERM has it stop: it finishes the step it is in, makes none of the steps left in its tick, and ends — within a second when it sleeps. No claim is released and no worker is stopped: the workers work on. Holding no claim, it takes its heartbeat off the remote; holding one, it leaves it with the claims, and the next start on this host takes them back. Its tick log keeps its `stop:` line, as ever. With `--all`, the host runner ends once every fleet instance has, and `stop` answers once it has ended.

The host runner's log has a line of each, beside the line of each fleet instance that ended:

```
checkout removed: /Users/me/Developments/hkj: by `afkconvoy stop`, its fleet instance stops
fleet instance ended: /Users/me/Developments/hkj: {"instance":"me-h1-1a2b3c4d","stopped":true,"ticks":12}
host runner told to stop by `afkconvoy stop --all`: it keeps the checkout list
host runner stopping: told to stop, each fleet instance ends its step
host runner stopped: 2 checkouts kept on the list
```

With no host runner running, `stop` takes the checkout off the list itself, and says so in that log; `--all` changes nothing.

##### What it answers

Once its fleet instance has stopped, with exit 0:

```json
{"checkout": "/Users/me/Developments/hkj", "repo": "github.com/me/hkj", "removed": true,
 "instance": "me-h1-1a2b3c4d", "stop": "stop: holding no claim, it took its heartbeat with it",
 "host_runner": {"pid": 4242, "version": "0.6.0", "log": "<cache>/host-runner.log",
                 "panel": "http://127.0.0.1:7070/"}}
```

- `removed`: false where the checkout was not on the list. Where no fleet instance of it ran either, nothing changed, and that is all it answers: a checkout not on the list exits 0.
- `instance` and `stop`: the fleet instance that stopped, and the `stop:` line its tick log keeps; null where none ran — the host runner could not start it, or no host runner runs.
- `host_runner`: the one that answered — its pid, its version, its log and where it serves the panel — or null where none runs. `<cache>` stands for the cache directory, whole in the answer.

With `--all`, once the host runner has ended:

```json
{"stopped": [{"checkout": "/Users/me/Developments/hkj", "instance": "me-h1-1a2b3c4d",
  "stop": "stop: it left its heartbeat with the claims it holds: the next start on this host takes them"}],
 "checkouts": 2,
 "host_runner": {"pid": 4242, "version": "0.6.0", "log": "<cache>/host-runner.log",
                 "panel": "http://127.0.0.1:7070/"}}
```

- `stopped`: each fleet instance it stopped, with its checkout, its id and its `stop:` line; [] where no host runner runs.
- `checkouts`: how many the list keeps: the next `run` starts each.

Errors, as {"error": …} with a non-zero exit: a second checkout of a repo on the list, naming the checkout to stop it from; the checkout list cannot be read or written; the host runner ended before it answered; its fleet instance did not stop within 10 minutes — it is off the list, and still finishing the step it is in; the host runner did not end within 30 seconds of answering `--all`. Each error a host runner gave says which, as `host_runner`.

##### What trips you up

- SIGTERM to the host runner's pid is `stop --all` but for the answer, and the line that says who told it. A second signal ends it at once, as SIGKILL does, with no goodbye.
- `stop` of the last checkout on the list leaves the host runner running, with none: the next `run` hands it its checkout.
- A `run` of a checkout whose fleet instance is stopping is refused until it has stopped. `stop` answers once it has: run it after.

##### Which checkout it is about

Name it after the command, as `[CHECKOUT]`: a checkout of the repo, or any directory in one, which names that checkout. Naming none, it is about the checkout it is run in. A worker's worktree is refused as its checkout: only a worker's own commands, and those that only read, are run there.

##### Usage

```
afkconvoy stop [OPTIONS] [CHECKOUT]
```

##### Arguments

- `[CHECKOUT]`: The checkout it is about, or a directory in it [default: the one it is run in]
- `--all`: Stop every fleet instance and then the host runner, keeping the checkout list

#### `afkconvoy panel`

Print the panel — every fleet of this host as one web page — as one rebuild of each checkout shows it now, or say where the host runner serves it live

##### When to run it

To see every fleet of this host at a glance where no host runner serves it: the host, what waits for a human across every repo, then each repo — its workflows as lines of stages, the issues at work, queued and held back at each. Save it and open it in a browser:

```
afkconvoy panel > panel.html                       every checkout on the checkout list
afkconvoy panel ~/Developments/hkj > hkj.html      that checkout alone
```

To watch the fleets, do not run this in a loop: the host runner serves the same page from its start, live — brought up to date after every tick of any fleet instance, by itself. Ask where:

```
afkconvoy panel --open
```

and open the address it answers. Run it again whenever you want that address back.

##### Who runs it

The operator, anywhere on the host. `--open` asks the host runner, whatever directory it is run in.

##### What it reads and writes

It writes nothing, on GitHub or on the remote, and makes no startup probe. For each checkout it makes the rebuild `plan` makes — the open issues and PRs, the claims and heartbeats, the base branch’s commits, and in a bound repo the team and every stage record — then asks orca after the worker of each claim of its fleet instance on this host, and reads its tick log on this host for the workers that are hot and whether its fleet instance is broken. Of the host it reads admission's reading, resource findings and the host watch, the exclusive queue, the host settings and the host kit.

With `--open` it reads nothing itself, and starts nothing: it asks this host's runner, on its socket, where it serves the panel. The host runner serves it from its start, to this host only, on the panel's port of the host settings — 7070 where they say none, or any free port where that one is taken (`afkconvoy run --help`).

##### What it answers

Not a JSON object: one HTML document on stdout, complete in itself, with no address in it that a browser would fetch. The same fleet state gives the same document. It has three parts, each made by one rendering, whether the host runner serves the page or this prints it:

- The host, once: admission — whether it holds back new workers, why, and what it read of the host; the workers that are hot, in every repo, with why and what each held at the most; the watch running, and what the last watch did; the commands run alone on the host and those waiting their turn (`exclusive`); host sleep — the sleep hours it may be put to sleep in, or that the host settings keep it awake, and which fleet instances are not idle; the host kit — each harness in order with its models, each one paused, and what the stock consult runs
- With a human, across every repo: each fleet instance that is broken, with why, since when and when the host runner starts it again; then every open issue that waits for a human, labelled with its repo, with what kind of wait and the first sentence of the reason its comment gives, a Reason link to that comment (the report itself for an older failed patrol or cut), and the line that answers it: what `doctor` answers as `waiting_on_human`. Also every open proposal on each bound repo's team's repo: its PR, source issue and ruling's comment, how long it has been open, and the exact merge and close commands — what `doctor` and `doctor --all` answer as `proposals.open`, including proposals whose source issue is closed. Once these reach the team's `max_open`, the page says so: further proposals wait at `full` (`afkconvoy help humans`)
- Each repo: a row at the top names every checkout, each with whether its fleet instance is idle, its claims held of its bound and its frontier, and links to its part. Each part then shows:
  - Claims held: the claims of its fleet instance that take a slot, of the concurrency
  - `Declared`: shown while there are any: the claims whose worker declared a verdict not acted on yet, which take no slot
  - a lane: one per workflow; an unbound repo has one, `backlog`, with the two stages `work` and `land`
  - a stage: the number in its stop is the workers at it; under it the issues at work — each with its worker's state: busy, stopped and for how long, or no worker — then the queued, which are the frontier, and in a bound repo those held back there, with why
  - `Patrols`: in a bound repo that names patrols: each, with what it is doing or what holds it back — one held by its `max_runs_a_day` says until when, as a time of day in UTC and how long from now
  - left alone: every other open issue, with the reason `plan` gives under `excluded`

Errors, as {"error": …} with a non-zero exit: the checkout list cannot be read; of a checkout named — or of the one it is run in, where the list holds none — the config, GitHub or the remote cannot be read. A checkout on the list that cannot be rebuilt is said so in its part, with why, and every other is shown.

With `--open`, one JSON object:

- `panel`: the address to open in a browser of this host: http://127.0.0.1:<port>/
- `host_runner`: the host runner that serves it: its pid, its version, its log, and that address as `panel`

Its errors, as {"error": …} with a non-zero exit, none of which changes anything:

- no host runner runs on this host: `afkconvoy run` starts one, which serves the panel; or print the page once, without `--open`
- the host runner did not answer within 10 seconds: its log says why
- the host runner serves no panel: it is of an older afkconvoy, which `afkconvoy run` moves onto this one; or it could not serve it, as its log says — or, for a fleet instance held in the foreground, as it warned

##### What trips you up

- Without `--instance` each checkout is seen as the fleet instance its tick log on this host names last — the one the host runner holds, or held — as the live page sees it; one whose fleet never ran on this host is seen as nobody's: its claims show as "held by <instance>", with no worker's state. `--instance` names the fleet instance of every checkout printed: name the checkout with it. `takeover --list` shows the ids.
- A worker's state is this host's orca's to say. A claim whose worker runs on another host shows "no worker" here.
- The panel is served at one address for as long as its host runner runs. `afkconvoy run --panel <port>` changes the port the next host runner serves it on, not the running one's: `afkconvoy stop --all` and then `afkconvoy run` moves it.
- A checkout a `run` adds is on the live page at once, as starting, and filled in by its first tick. One whose fleet instance broke shows what its last tick showed, said broken, until it is back.
- `--open` takes no checkout, no `--instance` and no `--host`: the page is the host runner's own.
- The page the host runner serves is not this one made again and again: each repo's part is made from what its fleet instance's tick already read, and adds what that tick did. It costs GitHub nothing.

##### Which checkout it is about

Name it after the command, as `[CHECKOUT]`: a checkout of the repo, or any directory in one, which names that checkout. Naming none, it is about every checkout on this host's checkout list — or, where the list holds none, the checkout it is run in. It only reads: a worker's worktree is one too.

##### Usage

```
afkconvoy panel [OPTIONS] [CHECKOUT]
```

##### Arguments

- `[CHECKOUT]`: The checkout it is about, or a directory in it [default: the one it is run in]
- `--instance <INSTANCE>`: The fleet instance whose claims are its own, of every checkout printed [default: the one its tick log on this host names last]
- `--host <HOST>`
- `--open`: Say where this host's runner serves the panel, live: nothing is started

#### `afkconvoy cast`

Choose a model within each issue's selected harness and add its `model:` label, in one session when enabled on this host

##### When to run it

Run `afkconvoy cast` in a repo to choose models now. Automatic casting is off by default, including after an upgrade. Enable it with `afkconvoy kit --cast on`; disable it with `afkconvoy kit --cast off`. The setting lives only in this host's kit, shared by all its checkouts.

##### Who runs it

The operator, in a checkout. An enabled tick also starts this command in the repo's convoy-caster worktree when an issue on the frontier needs a model.

##### What it reads and writes

Kit order and role eligibility choose the harness first. A choice means that some stage's selected harness holds multiple models in that role's range, with no matching model label already. A harness with zero or one model leaves no choice, regardless of later harnesses. An unbound issue carries the ready label, a bound issue a workflow's flow label; neither carries an epic label. Human casting labels keep an issue out of automatic recasting.

With casting off it explains that this host has not enabled it and sends no prompt. No tick holds an issue for casting. Workers still follow matching human model labels, otherwise the selected harness's first eligible model.

With casting on it sends one prompt about eligible issues to the host kit's first, using its login, and waits up to nine minutes. Each issue is offered only its stages' selected harnesses and eligible models still needing a choice, in kit order, with good_at and the roster's cast guidance. The answer is one JSON object per issue and selected harness: {issue, harness, model, why}.

Answers are checked against that issue's offered models and again against current kit priority, availability and labels. A valid answer adds only a model: label naming the model's id and a comment saying why. It writes no harness: label and removes no label. Legacy harness: labels never select a harness. A model: label applies only within a harness that holds it; other labels survive switches and faults and apply again when their harness is selected. A fallback can add its model beside an earlier caster label. Matching labels are reused without another session; human labels are never recast.

##### What it answers

{cast, uncast}: cast lists {issue, harness, model, why} for each added model label; uncast lists {issue, why} for unanswered or refused selections. Both are empty when casting is off or nothing needs a model, and said explains why; casting may list each issue's selection explanation. Errors: unreadable kit or team, or no answer from the selected questioner.

##### What trips you up

A tick waits at most ten minutes for its caster, then dispatches an unanswered issue on its range's first model. A changed candidate set opens a new choice; a live caster prevents a second one. Casting sends a real prompt and spends some of the login's allowance. Plan, doctor and panel show the host setting, each issue's casting reason, label matching, skipped models and actual running model. Switch alone leaves healthy workers on their current model; --all explicitly continues them.

##### Which checkout it is about

Name it after the command, as `[CHECKOUT]`: a checkout of the repo, or any directory in one, which names that checkout. Naming none, it is about the checkout it is run in. A worker runs it in its own worktree.

##### What it logs

As it acts it appends one line to the tick log of this host for this repo, then wakes this host's fleet instance of this repo, through the host runner; its answer says whether it woke one, as "woke": [`afkconvoy help tick-log`](help:tick-log).

##### Usage

```
afkconvoy cast [CHECKOUT]
```

##### Arguments

- `[CHECKOUT]`: The checkout it is about, or a directory in it [default: the one it is run in]

#### `afkconvoy switch`

Put a harness or model first in this machine's kit; optionally continue existing workers
